sections.title: Sets before formulas
sections.text: The intersection $A\cap B$ contains inputs allowed by both restrictions; the union $A\cup B$ allows either. The interval $[a,b)$ includes a and excludes $b$. A function assigns exactly one output to every member of its domain. Its codomain is the declared target set; its range consists of outputs actually attained.

sections.title: Set laws preserve membership
sections.text: For subsets of one universe, union and intersection are each commutative: $A\cup B=B\cup A$ and $A\cap B=B\cap A$. They are each associative: $A\cup(B\cup C)=(A\cup B)\cup C$ and likewise for $\cap$. Distribution works in both directions: $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$ and $A\cup(B\cap C)=(A\cup B)\cap(A\cup C)$. Check these by translating membership into “or” and “and”; changing parentheses never changes which member passes the test.

sections.title: Derive the domain
sections.text: For $f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}/(x-2)$, the root requires $x\geq 1$ and the denominator requires $x\ne 2$. Intersecting gives $[1,2)\cup (2,\infty )$. Declaring only $[3,4]$ as the domain defines a different, restricted function. A circle as a relation fails the function test where one input has two output heights.

exercise.prompt: Let $f:[-2,2]\to\mathbb R$ be $f(x)=x^2$. Identify domain, codomain and range. Can the same rule define a function into $[1,4]$?
exercise.hint: Check the output at $x=0$; then show that every value in your proposed range is attained.
exercise.solution: The domain is $[-2,2]$, codomain $\mathbb{R}$, and range $[0,4]$. Every $y$ in $[0,4]$ is attained at $x=\sqrt{y}$. The proposed codomain $[1,4]$ fails because $f(0)=0$ lies outside it.
rubric: Separate declared inputs from allowed outputs.
Prove both inclusion and attainment for the range.
Use an explicit input to refute the proposed codomain.

contentBlocks.title: Specify the set and its universe
items: A set contains distinct elements. List a small set, such as $S=\{1,3,5\}$, or describe it, such as $I=\{n\in\mathbb Z:n>0\}$. Membership $x\in S$ is a statement about one object.
Write $A\subseteq B$ only when every element of $A$ belongs to $B$. The empty set is a subset of every set; disjoint sets have empty intersection.
Fix a universe $U$ before taking complements: $A^{c}=U\setminus A$. A different $U$ can change the complement.

contentBlocks.title: Read operations as logical tests
contentBlocks.tex: x\in A\cup B\iff(x\in A\lor x\in B),\qquad x\in A\cap B\iff(x\in A\land x\in B),\qquad x\in A^c\iff(x\in U\land x\notin A)
contentBlocks.note: The “or” in a union includes elements in both sets. A complement is always relative to the chosen universe.

contentBlocks.title: Work one finite universe
contentBlocks.strategy: Test membership before writing each result; use an explicit witness to reject a subset claim.

steps.label: Subset and disjointness
steps.text: Every member of $A$ lies in $B$, so $A\subseteq B$. The sets are not disjoint because $1$ belongs to both.

steps.label: Union and intersection
steps.text: The shared members are $1$ and $3$; every member of either set is $1$, $2$, or $3$.

steps.label: Complement
steps.text: Subtract the members of $A$ from the specified universe, not from all integers.

contentBlocks.result: $2\in B$ but $2\notin A$, so $B\nsubseteq A$ even though $A\subseteq B$.
contentBlocks.verification: The complement changes if the universe changes: with $U^{\prime}=\{1,2,3,4,5\}$, it also contains $5$.

contentBlocks.title: Why the distributive law holds
contentBlocks.strategy: Show the same arbitrary element passes both membership tests.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $A,B,C$ be subsets of the same universe.

steps.label: Expand the left side
steps.text: $x\in A\cap(B\cup C)$ means $x\in A$ and at least one of $x\in B$ or $x\in C$.
steps.equation: x\in A\cap(B\cup C)\iff (x\in A)\land((x\in B)\lor(x\in C))

steps.label: Distribute the and
steps.text: This is equivalent to $x$ lying in both $A,B$ or in both $A,C$.

contentBlocks.result: $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$ by equality of members.
contentBlocks.verification: Replacing $(A\cap C)$ with $C$ is invalid: elements of $C$ outside $A$ would be added.

exercises.outcome: Translate a described set to a roster and decide membership.
exercises.prompt: In $U=\{-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}$, let $S=\{n\in U:n\text{ is odd}\}$. Enumerate $S$. Decide whether $0\in S$ and $3\in S$, and explain why writing $\{-1,1,3,3\}$ gives the same set.
exercises.hint: Test every member of the finite universe against “odd”. A set records membership, not repetition.
exercises.solution: The odd members of $U$ are $-1,1,3$, so $S=\{-1,1,3\}$. We have $0\notin S$ and $3\in S$. Repeating $3$ in a roster adds no new element.
rubric: Enumerate exactly the odd members of the stated universe.
Use membership symbols correctly for $0$ and $3$.
Explain that repeated entries do not change a set.

exercises.outcome: Compute set operations and a relative complement, and decide subset claims by a witness.
exercises.prompt: Let $U=\{0,1,2,3,4\}$, $A=\{0,2,4\}$, and $B=\{2,3\}$. Find $A\cap B$, $A\cup B$, $A^c$ relative to $U$, and $(A\cup B)^c$. Is $B\subseteq A$? Justify. Are $A$ and $B$ disjoint?
exercises.hint: For each element of $U$, mark membership in $A$ and $B$. A single counterexample settles a false subset claim.
exercises.solution: The only common element is $2$, so $A\cap B=\{2\}$. The union is $\{0,2,3,4\}$. Relative to $U$, $A^c=\{1,3\}$ and $(A\cup B)^c=\{1\}$. The subset claim fails because $3\in B$ but $3\notin A$. They are not disjoint because $2\in A\cap B$.
rubric: Use the stated $U$ for both complements.
Include $3$ in the union but not the intersection.
Give the member $3$ as a witness against $B\subseteq A$.
Use the shared member $2$ to reject disjointness.
exercises.solutionTex: A\cap B=\{2\},\quad A\cup B=\{0,2,3,4\},\quad A^c=\{1,3\},\quad(A\cup B)^c=\{1\}

exercises.outcome: Prove a set law by element membership and reject a tempting false variant.
exercises.prompt: Prove $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup(A\cap C)$ for subsets of one universe. Is $A\cap(B\cup C)=(A\cap B)\cup C$ always true? Give a counterexample if not.
exercises.hint: Start with an arbitrary $x$ and translate $\cap$ to “and” and $\cup$ to “or”. For the second claim, try an element of $C$ that is outside $A$.
exercises.solution: For any $x$, membership in the left side means $(x\in A)\land((x\in B)\lor(x\in C))$. Distributing gives $((x\in A)\land(x\in B))\lor((x\in A)\land(x\in C))$, exactly membership in the right side. For the false variant, take $A=\{1\}$, $B=\varnothing$, $C=\{2\}$ in $U=\{1,2\}$: the left side is empty but the proposed right side is $\{2\}$.
rubric: Prove both directions through an arbitrary member or an equivalent biconditional.
Keep $A$ in both intersection terms.
Give a concrete universe and contrasting results for the false variant.
exercises.solutionTex: x\in A\cap(B\cup C)\iff (x\in A\cap B)\lor(x\in A\cap C)

exercises.outcome: Use commutativity and associativity to rearrange a union without changing members.
exercises.prompt: For arbitrary sets $A,B,C$, justify $(A\cup B)\cup C=B\cup(A\cup C)$ by naming each law or by testing an arbitrary member. Does the same rearrangement hold with every $\cup$ replaced by $\cap$?
exercises.hint: First change the grouping; then swap $A$ and $B$. Both operations are available for union and intersection.
exercises.solution: Associativity gives $(A\cup B)\cup C=A\cup(B\cup C)$. Commutativity of the outer union gives $(B\cup C)\cup A$, and associativity/commutativity yield $B\cup(A\cup C)$. More directly, both sides contain exactly the members in at least one of $A,B,C$. The all-intersection statement also holds, because intersection is associative and commutative; both sides contain exactly the members in all three sets.
rubric: Name or demonstrate both associative and commutative steps.
Apply the same membership reasoning to intersection.
Do not invoke distributivity for a pure rearrangement.

sections.title: Classify with the domain
sections.text: Even means $f(-x)=f(x)$, odd means $f(-x)=-f(x)$, and either requires a domain symmetric about zero. Restricting $x^{2}$ to $[0,2]$ removes evenness under this convention. Increasing means $x_{1}<x_{2}$ implies $f(x_{1})\leq f(x_{2})$; strict increase replaces $\leq$ with $<$. The function $x^{3}$ is strictly increasing although its derivative vanishes at zero.

sections.title: Families and junctions
sections.text: Polynomials have real natural domains; rational functions exclude denominator zeros. Exponentials are positive, logarithms require positive inputs, and trigonometric domains depend on the function: $\tan$ excludes $\pi /2+k\pi$. For a piecewise function, inspect each formula on its assigned interval and compare both limiting heights with the actual junction value. The identity $|x|=-x$ for $x<0$ and $x$ for $x\geq 0$ makes its corner explicit.

exercise.prompt: Is $f(x)=x^3$ on $[-1,2]$ odd, strictly increasing, both, or neither?
exercise.hint: Test domain symmetry independently of the algebraic identity.
exercise.solution: It is strictly increasing, since $x_{1}^{3}<x_{2}^{3}$ whenever $x_{1}<x_{2}$. It is not odd under the symmetric-domain convention: 2 belongs to the domain but $-2$ does not.
rubric: State the domain convention.
Distinguish strict monotonicity from a derivative being everywhere positive.

sections.title: Track a point
sections.text: For $g(x)=a f(b(x-h))+k$ with $b\ne 0$, a point $(u,f(u))$ maps to $(h+u/b,k+a f(u))$. A negative $b$ reflects the input direction; a negative a reflects output heights. If $b=0$ and $f(0)$ exists, $g$ is constant a $f(0)+k$; the inverse point mapping is unavailable.

sections.title: Order changes the domain
sections.text: For $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $g(x)=x-1$, $f\circ g$ has domain $[1,\infty )$ and value $\sqrt{x-1}$. The reverse composition $g\circ f$ has domain $[0,\infty )$ and value $\sqrt{x}-1$. In each case require the inner input to exist and the inner output to belong to the outer domain.

exercise.prompt: If $(2,3)$ lies on $f$, where does it move under $g(x)=-2 f(-3(x-1))+4$?
exercise.hint: Solve $-3(x-1)=2$ before changing the output.
exercise.solution: The input is $x=1-2/3=1/3$; the output is $-2\cdot 3+4=-2$. The new point is $(1/3,-2)$.
rubric: Invert the input transformation.
Apply output scaling and translation in order.

contentBlocks.title: When a two-sided limit exists
contentBlocks.statement: A finite $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ exists if and only if the left and right limits both exist as finite numbers and equal $L$.
hypotheses: The domain has inputs approaching $a$ from both sides.
Each side is considered on a punctured neighbourhood; $f(a)$ does not enter the limit.
prerequisites: the left- and right-hand approach described in this lesson

contentBlocks.title: Why the two directions hold
contentBlocks.strategy: Restrict an approach to each side, then combine the two near-input conditions. The later precise-limits lesson gives the formal epsilon-delta version.
contentBlocks.setup: Assume inputs of the domain approach $a$ from both sides.

steps.label: Only if
steps.text: If outputs approach $L$ for every sufficiently near input, they also approach $L$ when we restrict inputs to either side.

steps.label: If
steps.text: Each side can bring outputs as close to $L$ as wanted. Use the smaller of the two allowable input distances; every sufficiently near input lies on one of those sides.

contentBlocks.result: Both directions give the stated equivalence for a finite limit.
contentBlocks.verification: The argument never uses the value at $a$ and needs approach points on both sides.

contentBlocks.title: Equal sides, missing point value
contentBlocks.strategy: Simplify only where the function is defined, then take each side's limit.

steps.label: Simplify
steps.text: For $x\ne1$, factor and cancel $x-1$; this says nothing about $f(1)$.

steps.label: Compare sides
steps.text: The simplified expression approaches 2 from below and above 1.

contentBlocks.result: The two-sided limit is 2 even though $f(1)$ is undefined.
contentBlocks.verification: Setting $f(1)=7$ changes continuity, not either one-sided limit.

contentBlocks.title: Unequal sides, no two-sided limit
contentBlocks.strategy: Evaluate the branch used on each side before asking about the value at the join.

steps.label: Approach from left
steps.text: The left branch approaches 1.

steps.label: Approach from right
steps.text: The right branch approaches 0.

contentBlocks.result: The limits disagree, so $\lim_{x\to0}g(x)$ does not exist.
contentBlocks.verification: Along $x=-1/n$, values tend to 1; along $x=1/n$, values tend to 0. Changing $g(0)$ cannot reconcile them.

sections.title: Four different failures
sections.text: A removable hole has equal finite one-sided limits but no matching point value. A jump has unequal one-sided limits. The function $1/x^{2}$ tends to $+\infty$ at zero, which is not a finite limit. The bounded function $\sin(1/x)$ oscillates: inputs approaching zero can give outputs 1 or $-1$.

sections.title: A rate with units
sections.text: If position is $s(t)=t^{2}$ metres with $t$ in seconds, average velocity over $[2,2+h]$ is $((2+h)^{2}-4)/h=4+h$ metres per second. As $h$ tends to zero from either side, velocity tends to 4 $m/s$. The $h=0$ quotient is undefined; its limit supplies the instantaneous rate.

exercise.prompt: For $f(x)=x+1$ when $x\ne 1$ and $f(1)=7$, find the limit at 1. Which point value makes $f$ continuous?
exercise.hint: The punctured neighborhood contains no information about $f(1)$.
exercise.solution: Both one-sided limits are 2. Setting $f(1)=2$ restores continuity. Changing only $f(1)$ cannot repair a jump with unequal one-sided limits.
rubric: Distinguish the limit from $f(1)$.
Explain why one-point repair needs a pre-existing finite limit.

exercises.outcome: Decide whether a two-sided limit exists when one one-sided limit fails.
exercises.prompt: Let $h(x)=x+2$ for $x<0$, $h(x)=\sin(1/x)$ for $x>0$, and $h(0)=2$. Does $\lim_{x\to0}h(x)$ exist? Explain using both sides, not only a plot or $h(0)$.
exercises.hint: The left limit is 2. On the right, find two positive sequences tending to zero whose sine values differ.
exercises.solution: From the left, $x+2\to2$. On the right, $x_n=1/(\pi/2+2\pi n)$ gives $h(x_n)=1$ and $y_n=1/(3\pi/2+2\pi n)$ gives $h(y_n)=-1$. Both sequences approach zero from the right, so the right-hand limit does not exist. Therefore the two-sided limit does not exist; $h(0)=2$ is irrelevant.
rubric: State the left-hand limit and identify that the right-hand limit fails to exist.
Give two right-side sequences with distinct limiting outputs or an equivalent proof of oscillation.
Do not use the point value as evidence for a punctured limit.

sections.title: Quantifiers and signs
sections.text: A right-hand limit of $+\infty$ at a means: for each $M>0$ there exists $\delta >0$ such that $0<x-a<\delta$ implies $f(x)>M$. Replace $f(x)>M$ by $f(x)<-M$ for $-\infty$. For $1/x$, the right limit at zero is $+\infty$ and the left limit is $-\infty$; for $1/x^{2}$ both are $+\infty$.

sections.title: Unbounded is weaker
sections.text: A denominator zero can be removable: $(x^{2}-1)/(x-1)$ has limit 2 at 1. The function $\sin(1/x)/x$ is unbounded near zero but does not tend to either infinity: along $x=1/(n\pi )$ its value is zero. A graph clipped at a finite height cannot certify an infinite limit.

exercise.prompt: Prove that $1/x^2$ tends to $+\infty$ as $x\to 0$.
exercise.hint: Given $M$, choose $\delta$ so that $\delta^{2}=1/M$.
exercise.solution: For $M>0$ choose $\delta =1/\sqrt{M}$. If $0<|x|<\delta$, then $x^{2}<1/M$, hence $1/x^{2}>M$. This works on both sides.
rubric: Choose $\delta$ after $M$.
Keep the puncture $0<|x|$.
Reverse the reciprocal inequality correctly.

supplementalBlocks.title: Prove the basic trigonometric limit in radians
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Compare areas of an inscribed triangle, a unit-circle sector, and a tangent triangle, then squeeze the ratio.
supplementalBlocks.setup: Take $0<x<\pi/2$ radians in a unit circle. The three areas are $\sin x/2$, $x/2$, and $\tan x/2$.

steps.label: Area order
steps.text: The inscribed triangle lies inside the sector, which lies inside the tangent triangle.
steps.usesHypothesis: Radian sector area is $x/2$; $0<x<\pi/2$ keeps all areas positive.

steps.label: Divide safely
steps.text: Since $\sin x>0$, divide and rearrange to trap the quotient.
steps.usesHypothesis: $x$ and $\sin x$ are nonzero in this punctured interval.

steps.label: Both sides
steps.text: $\cos x\to1$; squeeze from the right. Since $\sin(-x)/(-x)=\sin x/x$, the left limit agrees.

supplementalBlocks.verification: The angle must be in radians; degrees change the sector-area normalization.

supplementalBlocks.title: Rationalize before applying limit laws
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Replace a $0/0$ expression by an equal expression on the deleted domain.

steps.label: Conjugate
steps.text: Multiply numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{1+h}+1$.

steps.label: Pass to the limit
steps.text: The new denominator tends to 2, so its limit is nonzero.

supplementalBlocks.verification: The original expression is undefined at $h=0$; equality only on a deleted neighborhood suffices for the limit.

exercises.outcome: Use the proved sine limit and an identity to justify a new trigonometric limit.
exercises.prompt: Prove $\lim_{x\to0}(1-\cos x)/x^2=1/2$ in radians; name every nonzero denominator you introduce.
exercises.hint: Use $1-\cos x=\sin^2x/(1+\cos x)$ near zero.
exercises.solution: For nonzero $x$ sufficiently close to zero, $1+\cos x>0$. Then $(1-\cos x)/x^2=(\sin x/x)^2/(1+\cos x)$. The proved sine limit is $1$ and $\cos x\to1$, yielding $1/2$.
rubric: Use an identity valid near zero.
Check $x\ne 0$ and $1+\cos x\ne 0$.
Apply the sine limit in radians.

exercises.outcome: Rationalize a root limit while preserving its deleted domain.
exercises.prompt: Evaluate $\lim_{h\to0}(\sqrt{4+h}-2)/h$ and state where the original quotient is defined.
exercises.hint: Multiply by the conjugate before taking the limit.
exercises.solution: For $h\geq -4$ and $h\ne 0$, the quotient equals $1/(\sqrt{4+h}+2)$. Its denominator tends to 4, so the limit is $1/4$.
rubric: State $h\geq -4$ and $h\ne 0$.
Cancel only in the deleted domain.
Evaluate the nonzero limiting denominator.

sections.title: Eligibility before arithmetic
sections.text: The sum and product laws require the component finite limits to exist; the quotient law additionally requires a nonzero denominator limit. A quotient $0/0$ calls for another argument. Cancellation is valid in a punctured neighborhood even if the original expression is undefined at the target.

sections.title: Build an estimate
sections.text: Since $|\sin(1/x)|\le1$, $|x\sin(1/x)|\le|x|$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, taking $\delta=\varepsilon$ bounds the output error for every nonzero $|x|<\delta$. This establishes a limit without requiring the oscillating factor to have one.

exercise.prompt: Find $\lim_{x\to0}x^2\cos(1/x)$, justifying the estimate.
exercise.hint: Bound the absolute value by a non-oscillating function.
exercise.solution: The absolute value is at most $x^{2}$. For $\varepsilon >0$ use $\delta =\sqrt{\varepsilon }$. Then $0<|x|<\delta$ implies $|x^{2}\cos(1/x)|<\varepsilon$, so the limit is zero.
rubric: Use a bound valid for every nearby input.
Do not assign a limit to $\cos(1/x)$.

sections.title: The order matters
sections.text: The statement is: for every $\varepsilon >0$ there exists $\delta >0$ such that every allowed $x$ with $0<|x-a|<\delta$ satisfies $|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon$. The chosen $\delta$ may depend on $\varepsilon$ and a, but not on the particular $x$. Its negation has some $\varepsilon_{0}>0$ for which every $\delta >0$ admits a violating input.

sections.title: A nonlinear estimate
sections.text: To prove $x^{2}\to 4$ as $x\to 2$, factor $|x^{2}-4|=|x-2||x+2|$. First require $|x-2|<1$, giving $|x+2|<5$. Then choose $\delta=\min(1,\varepsilon/5)$. The same $\delta$ enforces both the local bound and the requested output tolerance.

exercise.prompt: Give a valid $\delta$ for proving $3x+2\to 5$ as $x\to 1$, and explain why it works.
exercise.hint: Express output error as a multiple of input error.
exercise.solution: Since $|(3x+2)-5|=3|x-1|$, choose $\delta =\varepsilon /3$. Every $0<|x-1|<\delta$ gives output error less than $\varepsilon$.
rubric: State that $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary and positive.
Choose $\delta$ independently of $x$.
Use strict inequalities consistently.

sections.title: Continuity depends on the domain
sections.text: At an endpoint of an interval, continuity is tested through the domain, so only the available side matters. At an interior point, existence of the finite limit and equality to the point value are both required.

sections.title: Existence is not uniqueness
sections.text: For $f(x)=x^{3}-x-1$, $f(1)=-1$ and $f(2)=5$. Polynomial continuity and the intermediate value theorem give a zero in $(1,2)$. This theorem alone does not count zeros. Bisection repeatedly retains an interval whose endpoint values bracket zero; discontinuity would invalidate its existence guarantee.

exercise.prompt: Why does a sign change in $f(x)=1/x$ between $-1$ and 1 not guarantee a zero?
exercise.hint: Which hypothesis fails on the closed interval?
exercise.solution: The function is not defined or continuous at zero, so IVT cannot be applied on $[-1,1]$. Indeed $1/x$ is never zero on its domain.
rubric: Check the entire interval, not just its endpoints.
Separate a failed theorem application from the truth of its conclusion.

sections.title: Derive before substituting
sections.text: For $f(x)=x^{2}$, the secant quotient at a is $((a+h)^{2}-a^{2})/h=2a+h$ for $h\ne 0$. The derivative is the limit 2a. On the graph, the secant line uses two distinct points; the tangent is the limiting line, not a zero-length secant.

sections.title: Two derivative functions
sections.text: A derivative at a is a number. The derivative function $f'$ assigns that number to every point where the limit exists. If $f$ measures metres and $x$ seconds, $f'$ measures metres per second; a second derivative measures metres per second squared.

exercise.prompt: Use the definition to differentiate $f(x)=1/x$ at $a\ne 0$.
exercise.hint: Combine the fractions before cancelling $h$; keep $a+h$ nonzero.
exercise.solution: The quotient is $(1/(a+h)-1/a)/h=-1/(a(a+h))$. As $h\to 0$ this tends to $-1/a^{2}$. Choose a neighborhood with $|h|<|a|/2$ to keep denominators nonzero.
rubric: Show the algebraic cancellation only for $h\ne 0$.
State $a\ne 0$ and control nearby denominators.

contentBlocks.title: Differentiate the derivative by its own limit
contentBlocks.strategy: Find the first derivative, then form a fresh difference quotient for that derivative.
contentBlocks.setup: For $f(x)=x^3-x$, find $f''(x)$ from the definition, as in Lecture 06 Example 6.

steps.label: First derivative
steps.text: Expand $f(x+h)-f(x)$ and divide only for $h\ne0$.

steps.label: New quotient
steps.text: Apply the derivative definition to $f'$, rather than taking the old quotient's limit twice.

steps.label: Second limit
steps.text: Now let the nonzero increment tend to zero.

contentBlocks.result: $f''(x)=6x$ is the rate of change of $f'(x)$.
contentBlocks.verification: Both quotients are defined only for $h\ne0$; a second derivative exists here because $f'$ is differentiable everywhere.

supplementalBlocks.title: Higher derivatives track different rates
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Differentiate the position function successively; interpret each derivative with its own units.

steps.label: Velocity
steps.text: Differentiate position once.

steps.label: Acceleration
steps.text: Differentiate velocity, not position again by a new rule.

steps.label: At one second
steps.text: $v(1)=-3 m/s$ and $a(1)=0 m/s^{2}$. Zero acceleration at an instant does not mean zero velocity.

supplementalBlocks.result: At $t=1$, motion is in the negative direction at 3 $m/s$ while acceleration vanishes.
supplementalBlocks.verification: $a(t)$ changes sign at 1; it is not identically zero near that time.

exercises.outcome: Compute a second derivative by taking the difference-quotient limit of the first derivative.
exercises.prompt: For $g(x)=x^3+2x^2$, first find $g'(x)$. Then use $\lim_{h\to0}(g'(x+h)-g'(x))/h$ to find $g''(x)$; show the quotient before taking its limit.
exercises.hint: After $g'(x)=3x^2+4x$, expand $g'(x+h)$ and cancel the matching terms before dividing by nonzero $h$.
rubric: Find the first derivative before forming the new quotient.
Show cancellation for $h\ne0$ before taking the limit.
Conclude $g''(x)=6x+4$, not $g'(x)$ again.

exercises.outcome: Compute and interpret first and second derivatives separately.
exercises.prompt: A particle has position $s(t)=t^4-4t^3$ metres for $t\ge0$. Find velocity and acceleration at $t=2$, and decide whether it is instantaneously at rest.
exercises.hint: Differentiate once for velocity and twice for acceleration; rest means velocity zero.
exercises.solution: $v(t)=4t^3-12t^2$, so $v(2)=32-48=-16 m/s$. $a(t)=12t^2-24t$, so $a(2)=0 m/s^{2}$. The particle is moving, not at rest.
rubric: Differentiate in the right order.
Keep units for each derivative.
Use velocity, not acceleration, to decide rest.

sections.title: A second derivative requires a new limit
sections.text: If $f'$ is differentiable at $x$, its derivative is $f''(x)=\lim_{h\to0}(f'(x+h)-f'(x))/h$. Existence of $f'(x)$ alone does not guarantee this second limit. The notation $d^2y/dx^2$ means differentiating $dy/dx$ once more, not squaring it.

sections.title: Three obstructions
sections.text: For $|x|$ at zero, the difference quotient is $-1$ from the left and 1 from the right: a corner. For $x^{1/3}$, its quotient at zero is $|h|^{-2/3}$, which has no finite limit: a vertical tangent does not supply a finite derivative. A discontinuity also prevents differentiability.

sections.title: Why differentiability implies continuity
sections.text: Write $f(a+h)-f(a)=h\cdot ((f(a+h)-f(a))/h)$. If the quotient has a finite limit, multiplying by $h\to 0$ gives an increment tending to zero. The converse fails, as $|x|$ demonstrates.

exercise.prompt: Is $f(x)=|x-2|$ differentiable at 2? State the one-sided quotients.
exercise.hint: Set $x=2+h$.
exercise.solution: The quotient $|h|/h$ equals $-1$ for $h<0$ and 1 for $h>0$. It has no two-sided limit, although $f$ is continuous at 2.
rubric: Compute the two signs.
Distinguish continuity from differentiability.

supplementalBlocks.title: Build the algebraic families
supplementalBlocks.note: These formulas require the displayed derivatives to exist. The quotient also requires $g(x)\ne0$; for general real powers use a domain where the power is differentiable.

supplementalBlocks.title: Why both factors contribute
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Add and subtract one mixed product before dividing by the input increment.

steps.label: Split
steps.text: Insert $f(x+h)g(x)$ into the numerator.

steps.label: Limit
steps.text: Differentiability gives $f(x+h)\to f(x)$ and both quotient limits.
steps.usesHypothesis: Differentiability of both factors at $x$ implies continuity there.

supplementalBlocks.title: Trigonometric derivatives in radians
supplementalBlocks.tex: \begin{aligned}(\sin x)'&=\cos x &(\cos x)'&=-\sin x\\(\tan x)'&=\sec^2x &(\cot x)'&=-\csc^2x\\(\sec x)'&=\sec x\tan x &(\csc x)'&=-\csc x\cot x\end{aligned}
supplementalBlocks.note: The sine and cosine derivatives use the radian sine limit. Tangent and secant require $\cos x\ne0$; cotangent and cosecant require $\sin x\ne0$. The quotient rule yields the latter four from sine and cosine.

exercises.outcome: Differentiate a product while retaining both changing contributions.
exercises.prompt: Differentiate $x^2\sin x$ and check the derivative at $x=\pi$ without graphing.
exercises.hint: Treat $x^2$ and $\sin x$ as separate factors.
exercises.solution: The derivative is $2x\sin x+x^2\cos x$. At $x=\pi$ it is $-\pi^2$ because $\sin\pi=0$ and $\cos\pi=-1$.
rubric: Differentiate both factors.
Keep the original companion factor in each term.
Evaluate the trig values in radians.

exercises.outcome: Derive a trigonometric derivative with its domain rather than memorizing it.
exercises.prompt: Derive $(\tan x)'=\sec^2x$ from $\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$. State its domain.
exercises.hint: Use the quotient rule and $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$.
exercises.solution: When $\cos x\ne0$, the quotient rule gives $(\cos^2x+\sin^2x)/\cos^2x=1/\cos^2x=\sec^2x$. The derivative is only defined where $x\ne\pi/2+k\pi$ for integer $k$.
rubric: Apply quotient numerator order correctly.
Use the Pythagorean identity.
Exclude zeros of cosine.

sections.title: Choose the outer operation
sections.text: A product differentiates as $f'g+fg'$; a quotient as $(f'g-fg')/g^2$ where $g\ne0$. In radians, $(\sin x)'=\cos x$ and $(\cos x)'=-\sin x$. The expression $x\sin x$ is a product, so its derivative is $\sin x+x\cos x$.

sections.title: A quotient worked through
sections.text: For $q(x)=\sin x/x$ on $x\ne0$, numerator derivative is $\cos x$ and denominator derivative is $1$. Thus $q'(x)=(x\cos x-\sin x)/x^2$. The derivative formula has the same excluded zero; any extension at zero must be defined and differentiated separately.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $(x^2+1)/(x-1)$ and state its domain.
exercise.hint: Use the quotient rule with the numerator derivative 2x.
rubric: Preserve the minus sign before the entire numerator.
Square the denominator.
State $x\ne 1$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Keep the zero inner increment case
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Express both differentiability errors with coefficients that tend to zero; avoid dividing by the inner increment.

steps.label: Inner estimate
steps.text: $k=g'(a)h+o(h)$, so $k/h$ stays bounded as $h\to0$.

steps.label: Outer estimate
steps.text: $f(u+k)-f(u)=f'(u)k+k\eta(k)$, including $k=0$.

steps.label: Combine
steps.text: The error divided by $h$ is $f'(u)(k/h-g'(a))+\eta(k)(k/h)$; both terms tend to zero.

supplementalBlocks.result: $(f\circ g)'(a)=f'(g(a))g'(a)$, even when $g'(a)=0$ or some nonzero $h$ gives $k=0$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: No step divides by $k$, so a locally flat inner function causes no gap.

exercises.outcome: Apply the chain rule when the inner derivative vanishes without invalid division.
exercises.prompt: For $g(x)=x^2$ and differentiable $f$ at 0, find $(f\circ g)'(0)$. Explain why dividing a difference quotient by $g(h)-g(0)$ is unsafe as a general proof step.
exercises.hint: Use $f(k)=f(0)+f'(0)k+o(k)$ with $k=h^2$.
exercises.solution: The increment is $f(h^{2})-f(0)=f'(0)h^{2}+o(h^{2})$. Dividing by $h$ gives $f'(0)h+o(h)\to 0$. A general $g$ can have $g(a+h)=g(a)$ for some nonzero $h$, so dividing by its increment may be undefined; the remainder proof avoids it.
rubric: Use the outer differentiability at zero.
Obtain derivative zero.
Explain the zero-increment division issue.

sections.title: Make little-o explicit
sections.text: The notation $r(h)=o(h)$ means $r(h)/h\to 0$. Differentiability of $g$ at a says $g(a+h)=g(a)+g'(a)h+o(h)$. Differentiability of $f$ at $g(a)$ lets its output increment be $f'(g(a))$ times the inner increment plus a smaller error. Combining gives derivative $f'(g(a))g'(a)$; the argument also covers $g'(a)=0$.

sections.title: Layers and domains
sections.text: For $y=\sin(x^{2})$, the outer function is $\sin$ and the inner is $x^{2}$, giving $y'=\cos(x^{2})\cdot 2x$. For $\ln(1+x^{2})$, divide the inner derivative 2x by the positive inner value $1+x^{2}$. Naming layers prevents replacing $\cos(x^{2})$ by $\cos x$.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $(1+\sin x)^3$.
exercise.hint: Differentiate the cube with respect to its input, then multiply by the derivative of that input.
exercise.solution: The derivative is $3(1+\sin x)^2\cos x$, for every real $x$.
rubric: Keep the full inner expression in the squared factor.
Include the inner derivative.

sections.title: Differentiate an identity on a branch
sections.text: From $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$, assuming a differentiable local branch $y(x)$, differentiate to get $2x+2yy'=0$. Where $y\ne 0$, $y'=-x/y$. At $(3,4)$ the tangent slope is $-3/4$. At $y=0$ this formula cannot solve for $y'$; a different local graph may be needed.

sections.title: Rates carry units
sections.text: For a spherical balloon $V=(4\pi /3)r^{3}$, differentiation in time gives $dV/dt=4\pi r^{2} dr/dt$. If $dV/dt=12\pi cm^{3}/s$ at $r=3$ cm, then $dr/dt=1/3 cm/s$. Substitute the instantaneous radius after differentiating, since it varies in time.

exercise.prompt: A 5 $m$ ladder has foot distance $x$ and height $y$ with $x^2+y^2=25$. At $x=3$ $m$ its foot moves outward at 2 $m/s$. Find $dy/dt$.
exercise.hint: Use $y=4$ and differentiate with respect to time.
exercise.solution: 2x $dx/dt+2y dy/dt=0$, so $dy/dt=-(3/4)\cdot 2=-3/2 m/s$. The negative sign means the top descends.
rubric: Differentiate both changing quantities.
Use the positive height.
Interpret sign and units.

supplementalBlocks.title: Read the remainder notation precisely
items: $R(h)=O(h^2)$ means there are $C,\delta>0$ with $|R(h)|\le C|h|^2$ whenever $0<|h|<\delta$.
An $O(h^2)$ bound implies $o(|h|)$, but a bare $o(|h|)$ statement supplies no fixed quadratic constant.

supplementalBlocks.title: One exact error, two kinds of control
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Subtract the affine model and compare the residual with powers of the step.

steps.label: Model
steps.text: $f(1)=1$ and $f'(1)=2$, so the affine approximation is $1+2h$.

steps.label: Residual
steps.text: The exact remainder is $h^2$.

supplementalBlocks.verification: For a specified tolerance $\varepsilon$, $|h|<\sqrt\varepsilon$ ensures the exact error $h^2<\varepsilon$.

exercises.outcome: Distinguish a uniform quadratic bound from first-order asymptotic smallness.
exercises.prompt: For $R(h)=|h|^{3/2}$, decide whether $R(h)=o(|h|)$ and whether $R(h)=O(h^2)$ as $h\to0$. Justify each answer from a ratio or bound.
exercises.hint: Compare $R(h)/|h|$ and $R(h)/h^2$ separately.
exercises.solution: $R(h)/|h|=|h|^{1/2}\to 0$, so $R=o(|h|)$. But $R(h)/h^{2}=1/\sqrt{|h|}$ is unbounded near zero, so no fixed $C$ gives $R\leq C h^{2}$ on a deleted neighborhood; $R$ is not $O(h^{2})$.
rubric: Check each notation by its own definition.
Use a deleted neighborhood.
Do not infer a quadratic bound from little-o of first order.

sections.title: Linear versus affine
sections.text: The derivative is the linear map $h\mapsto f'(a)h$. The approximating graph $x\mapsto f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$ is affine because it includes an offset. Differentiability guarantees error $o(|x-a|)$, not a chosen finite error bound for arbitrary steps.

sections.title: Approximate with an error bound
sections.text: For $\sqrt{x}$ near $a=4$, $L(x)=2+(x-4)/4$, so $L(4.1)=2.025$. Taylor’s theorem gives error at most $M(0.1)^{2}/2$ if $|f''|\leq M$ between 4 and 4.1. Here $|f''|=1/(4x^{3/2}) \leq 1/32$, so the error is at most 0.00015625. This finite bound is stronger than a bare little-o statement.

exercise.prompt: Use linearization at 0 to approximate $\sin(0.02)$. What extra information would certify an error bound?
exercise.hint: Use $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$; a remainder estimate needs derivative control.
exercise.solution: The linear estimate is 0.02. Taylor’s theorem and $|\sin''x|\leq 1$ give error at most $(0.02)^{2}/2=0.0002$. A sharper cubic bound is possible using additional vanishing terms.
rubric: Identify the base point.
Separate approximation from equality.
State the theorem and derivative bound for the error.

sections.title: A convention for candidates
sections.text: Here a critical point is an interior domain point where $f'=0$ or $f'$ does not exist; a stationary point has $f'=0$. Endpoints are checked separately. Fermat’s theorem says that a differentiable interior local extremum is stationary, not that every stationary point is an extremum.

sections.title: List, then compare
sections.text: For $f(x)=x^{3}-3x$ on $[-2,2]$, $f'=3x^{2}-3$ vanishes at $\pm 1$. Evaluate endpoints and stationary points: $f(-2)=-2$, $f(-1)=2$, $f(1)=-2$, $f(2)=2$. The global minimum is $-2$ at $-2$ and 1; the maximum is 2 at $-1$ and 2. Compactness and continuity ensure attainment.

exercise.prompt: Why does $f(x)=x$ on $[0,1]$ have a maximum even though $f'$ never vanishes?
exercise.hint: Is the maximum an interior point?
exercise.solution: The maximum is $f(1)=1$ at an endpoint. Fermat’s necessary condition applies only to differentiable interior extrema, so there is no contradiction.
rubric: State endpoint eligibility.
Do not infer no extrema from no stationary points.

contentBlocks.title: Rolle’s theorem
contentBlocks.statement: If $f(a)=f(b)$, some $c$ strictly between $a$ and $b$ has $f'(c)=0$.

contentBlocks.title: Why Rolle’s point exists
contentBlocks.strategy: Use an attained extremum; equal endpoint values force a nonconstant function’s relevant extremum inside.

steps.label: Attainment
steps.text: Continuity on the closed interval gives both a maximum and a minimum.

steps.label: Interior point
steps.text: If $f$ is constant, choose any $c\in(a,b)$. Otherwise a value differs from $k$, so the maximum or minimum in that direction cannot occur at either endpoint.

steps.label: Stationarity
steps.text: At that interior extremum, Fermat’s theorem gives $f'(c)=0$.

contentBlocks.verification: The constant case also has derivative zero at every interior point.

contentBlocks.title: Subtract the secant
contentBlocks.strategy: Make an equal-endpoint function and apply Rolle’s theorem.

steps.label: Endpoint check
steps.text: $g(a)=g(b)=0$ by the definition of $m$.

steps.label: Apply Rolle
steps.text: $g$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, so $g'(c)=0$ for some interior $c$.
steps.usesHypothesis: Both regularity hypotheses on $f$; subtracting a linear function preserves them.

steps.label: Recover the slope
steps.text: Since $g'(c)=f'(c)-m$, its vanishing gives the required secant slope.

contentBlocks.verification: When $f(a)=f(b)$, the formula reduces to Rolle’s zero-slope conclusion.

contentBlocks.title: Locate the matching tangent
contentBlocks.strategy: Compute the secant slope, then solve the derivative equation within the interval.

steps.label: Eligibility
steps.text: A polynomial is continuous and differentiable on the required intervals; $b>0$ makes this a nondegenerate interval.

steps.label: Secant
steps.text: The average slope is $b$.

steps.label: Tangent
steps.text: Solve $2c=b$, giving $c=b/2$.

exercises.outcome: Use the mean value theorem to prove a global consequence from local slopes.
exercises.prompt: Let $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'(x)=0$ throughout $(a,b)$. Prove $f$ is constant on $[a,b]$.
exercises.hint: Choose arbitrary $u<v$ in the interval. Apply the theorem on $[u,v]$.
exercises.solution: For any $u<v$ in $[a,b]$, MVT gives $c\in(u,v)$ with $(f(v)-f(u))/(v-u)=f'(c)=0$. Thus $f(v)=f(u)$. Since the pair was arbitrary, $f$ is constant.
rubric: Apply MVT to arbitrary points, not only the original endpoints.
State continuity and differentiability on the chosen subinterval.
Conclude equality of all values.

sections.title: Rolle’s theorem supplies the bridge
sections.text: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f(a)=f(b)$, extrema are attained. If $f$ is constant, any interior point has derivative zero. Otherwise a value differs from the common endpoint value, so a maximum or minimum occurs inside; Fermat gives derivative zero there.

sections.title: Subtract the secant
sections.text: Set $g(x)=f(x)-f(a)-m(x-a)$, where $m=(f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)$. Then $g(a)=g(b)=0$. Rolle provides $c$ with $g'(c)=0$, hence $f'(c)=m$. For $f(x)=x^{2}$ on $[1,3]$, $m=4$ and $c=2$.

exercise.prompt: Why can the mean value theorem not be used for $|x|$ on $[-1,1]$?
exercise.hint: Check differentiability at the interior junction.
exercise.solution: The endpoint slope is zero, but $|x|$ is not differentiable at zero and its derivative elsewhere is $\pm 1$. The missing differentiability hypothesis prevents the claimed conclusion.
rubric: Name the failed hypothesis and its location.
Compute the secant and available derivatives.

sections.title: Continuity is indispensable
sections.text: The derivative signs constrain nearby motion but do not fix a separately assigned point height. The example $f(x)=-|x|$ for $x\ne 0$ with $f(0)=-1$ has the positive-to-negative derivative pattern and nevertheless a strict local minimum at zero.

sections.title: Zero second derivative gives no verdict
sections.text: At zero, $x^{4}$ has a strict minimum, $-x^{4}$ a strict maximum, and $x^{3}$ neither, although all three have first and second derivatives zero there. Check derivative signs or the original value comparison. An inflection point requires a change of concavity, not merely $f''=0$.

exercise.prompt: Classify $x^4$ at zero without using an inconclusive second-derivative test.
exercise.hint: Compare $f(x)$ with $f(0)$ for nonzero $x$.
exercise.solution: For $x\ne 0$, $x^{4}>0=f(0)$, so zero is a strict global and local minimum. Equivalently $f'=4x^{3}$ changes from negative to positive.
rubric: Identify why the second-derivative test is inconclusive.
Supply a direct inequality or valid sign test.

sections.title: Separate the two tails
sections.text: For rational functions, divide by the highest denominator power separately as $x\to +\infty$ and $x\to -\infty$. For $\sqrt{x^{2}+1}/x$, factoring produces $|x|/x$ times $\sqrt{1+1/x^{2}}$, giving limits 1 and $-1$. Replacing $\sqrt{x^{2}}$ by $x$ would lose the negative tail.

sections.title: A sketch is an assembled argument
sections.text: For $f(x)=x+1/x$, domain excludes zero. Its slant asymptote is $y=x$ because $f(x)-x\to 0$ at both infinities. Derivative $1-1/x^{2}$ is positive for $|x|>1$ and negative for $0<|x|<1$; stationary points are $-1$ and 1. Add the separate vertical behavior at zero before drawing connected pieces.

exercise.prompt: Find the slant asymptote of $(x^2+1)/(x-1)$.
exercise.hint: Perform polynomial division.
exercise.solution: $(x^{2}+1)/(x-1)=x+1+2/(x-1)$. The remainder tends to zero at either infinity, so $y=x+1$ is the slant asymptote; $x=1$ remains excluded.
rubric: Show the vanishing difference.
Keep the finite-domain restriction separate.

sections.title: Model the feasible set
sections.text: A rectangle with perimeter 20 has $y=10-x$ and area $A=x(10-x)$. Positive side lengths require $0<x<10$; including degenerate rectangles closes the set to $[0,10]$. Differentiate A to get $10-2x$, whose zero is $x=5$. Then $y=5$ and $A=25$.

sections.title: Justify a global answer
sections.text: The identity $A=25-(x-5)^{2}$ proves $A\leq 25$ throughout the feasible set. This proves global optimality directly, whereas a positive-to-negative sign change by itself describes local behavior. Check units: perimeter in metres gives area in square metres.

exercise.prompt: Find the largest area rectangle with perimeter $P>0$.
exercise.hint: Eliminate one side and complete the square.
exercise.solution: With $y=P/2-x$, $A=x(P/2-x)=P^{2}/16-(x-P/4)^{2}$. Its maximum $P^{2}/16$ occurs at $x=y=P/4$, within the positive feasible interval.
rubric: State positivity and the feasible interval.
Prove global optimality.
Retain units and parameter dependence.

sections.title: Derive the update
sections.text: The tangent at $x_n$ has equation $y=f(x_{n})+f'(x_{n})(x-x_{n})$. Setting $y=0$ gives $x_{n+1}=x_{n}-f(x_{n})/f'(x_{n})$, provided the derivative is nonzero. It finds a tangent intercept, not an exact root of the original curve.

sections.title: Failure deserves an example
sections.text: For $f(x)=x^{3}-2x+2$, starting at 0 gives 1 and starting at 1 gives 0, so Newton cycles. For $x^{2}-2$, starting at zero is undefined because $f'(0)=0$. A small step alone is not proof of a root; check the residual and the domain, and use a bracket when available.

exercise.prompt: Perform two Newton steps for $x^2-2$ from $x_0=1$.
exercise.solution: $x_{1}=3/2$ and $x_{2}=17/12$. The residual at the second iterate is $(17/12)^{2}-2=1/144$; it is an approximation, not an exact root.
rubric: Calculate both steps.
Check the residual.
Avoid claiming universal convergence.

sections.title: Why the constant is the only freedom
sections.text: If $F'=G'$ on an interval, then $(F-G)'=0$. Applying MVT between any two points gives equal values of $F-G$. Thus $F-G$ is constant on that interval. On a disconnected domain the constants may differ between components.

sections.title: Use initial data
sections.text: If velocity is $v(t)=3t^{2}-2$ and $s(0)=5$, integrating gives $s(t)=t^{3}-2t+C$. The initial value sets $C=5$. Differentiation recovers the velocity and checks the answer; the constant carries position units.

exercise.prompt: Find every antiderivative of $1/x$ on $\mathbb R$ excluding zero.
exercise.hint: Treat the negative and positive intervals separately.
exercise.solution: The answer is ${\ln|x|+C_-}$ for $x<0$ and ${\ln|x|+C_+}$ for $x>0$, with independent constants. No interval in this domain connects the two sides.
rubric: Use $\ln|x|$, not $\ln x$ on negative inputs.
Allow separate constants on disconnected components.

contentBlocks.title: Existence of an inverse
contentBlocks.statement: A continuous strictly monotone function on an interval has an inverse on its range.
hypotheses: $f$ is continuous and strictly monotone on it.
prerequisites: Continuity and the intermediate value theorem

contentBlocks.title: Local inverse derivative theorem
contentBlocks.statement: Near $a$, the inverse exists and is differentiable near $f(a)$; at a corresponding input, $(f^{-1})'(f(a))=1/f'(a)$.

contentBlocks.title: Differentiate after existence is known
contentBlocks.strategy: Use the inverse identity only after the theorem supplies a differentiable inverse.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $y=f(x)$ on the local branch, so $x=f^{-1}(y)$.

steps.label: Identity
steps.text: On that branch $f(f^{-1}(y))=y$.

steps.label: Chain rule
steps.text: Differentiate the identity where the inverse is differentiable.
steps.usesHypothesis: The imported local inverse derivative theorem; this calculation does not prove existence.

steps.label: Divide
steps.text: The derivative at the corresponding input is nonzero, so division is valid.

contentBlocks.verification: For $f(x)=x^3$, $f'(0)=0$ and its inverse cube root has no finite derivative at zero; the hypothesis matters.

contentBlocks.title: Differentiate an inverse at an output
contentBlocks.strategy: Find the input first, check the theorem’s conditions, then take the reciprocal slope.

steps.label: Eligibility
steps.text: $f'(x)=3x^2+1>0$ everywhere, so $f$ is strictly increasing and the derivative is nonzero.

steps.label: Reciprocal
steps.text: $f'(1)=4$; the inverse slope at output 2 is its reciprocal.

contentBlocks.verification: The reciprocal is evaluated at input 1, not at output 2.

exercises.outcome: Choose an inverse branch before using the derivative formula.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x)=x^2$ on all real numbers, a student writes $(f^{-1})'(4)=1/4$. Explain the problem. Give the inverse derivative at 4 on each monotone branch.
exercises.hint: One output has two inputs. Restrict the domain to $[0,\infty)$ or $(-\infty,0]$ first.
exercises.solution: There is no inverse function on all real inputs: 4 comes from both 2 and $-2$. On the nonnegative branch the inverse is $\sqrt{y}$, with derivative $1/(2\sqrt4)=1/4$. On the nonpositive branch the inverse is $-\sqrt{y}$, with derivative $-1/4$ at 4.
rubric: Identify the lack of injectivity on the original domain.
Name each branch and its range.
Keep the negative branch’s derivative sign.

sections.title: Existence precedes the derivative
sections.text: A continuous strictly monotone function on an interval has an inverse on its range. A sufficient local differentiability theorem assumes $f$ is continuously differentiable near a and $f'(a)\ne 0$; then its local inverse is differentiable near $f(a)$. Only after this theorem may differentiating $f(f^{-1}(y))=y$ establish $(f^{-1})'(y)=1/f'(f^{-1}(y))$.

sections.title: Zero derivative is a warning
sections.text: The inverse of $x^{3}$ is the cube root. Although $x^{3}$ is one-to-one, its derivative at zero vanishes and the inverse has no finite derivative there. For $x^{2}$, choose a branch such as $[0,\infty )$ before naming $\sqrt{x}$ as its inverse.

exercise.prompt: For $f(x)=x^3+x$, find the derivative of its inverse at $y=2$.
exercise.hint: Find the input mapped to 2, then evaluate $f'$ there.
exercise.solution: $f(1)=2$ and $f'(1)=3+1=4$, so $(f^{-1})'(2)=1/4$. Since $f'=3x^{2}+1>0$, the inverse is well-defined and differentiable.
rubric: Evaluate at the inverse input, not at $y$ directly.
Check the derivative is nonzero.

sections.title: A definition must have a foundation
sections.text: One rigorous route defines $\ln x$ as the integral from $1$ to $x$ of $1/t$ for $x>0$, then uses the fundamental theorem to obtain derivative $1/x$. Its inverse is $\exp$; the inverse derivative theorem yields $\exp'=\exp$. If integration has not been developed yet, these facts are imported theorems.

sections.title: Logarithmic differentiation
sections.text: For $y=x^{x}$ on $x>0$, take $\ln y=x\ln x$. Differentiate to obtain $y'/y=\ln x+1$, hence $y'=x^{x}(\ln x+1)$. The positive domain permits logarithms; this argument does not define a real differentiable $x^x$ on all negative inputs.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $\ln(x^2-1)$ over its real domain.
exercise.hint: First require $x^{2}-1>0$.
exercise.solution: The domain is $(-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty )$. The derivative is $2x/(x^{2}-1)$ on that domain.
rubric: Solve the strict domain inequality.
Include the inner derivative.

supplementalBlocks.title: A one-sided $0/0$ rule
supplementalBlocks.statement: If $f/g$ has $0/0$ form at $a$ and $f'(x)/g'(x)\to L$, then $f(x)/g(x)\to L$ from the same side under the listed conditions.
hypotheses: $f$ and $g$ are continuous to $a$ from that side, with $f(a)=g(a)=0$.
$f$ and $g$ are differentiable on a deleted one-sided interval.
$g'(x)\ne0$ there and the derivative ratio has a finite or signed infinite limit $L$.

supplementalBlocks.title: Where Cauchy’s theorem enters
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Compare each nearby point with the endpoint at which both functions vanish.
supplementalBlocks.setup: For $x$ on the chosen side of $a$, apply Cauchy’s mean value theorem to $f,g$ on the interval between $a$ and $x$.

steps.label: Intermediate point
steps.text: There is $c_x$ between $a$ and $x$ with $f(x)g'(c_x)=g(x)f'(c_x)$.
steps.usesHypothesis: Continuity up to the endpoint and differentiability inside; both endpoint values are zero.

steps.label: Divide
steps.text:
$g'(c_x)
e0$; Cauchy’s relation and the mean value theorem for $g$ make $g(x)
e0$ for $x
e a$.

steps.label: Limit
steps.text: As $x\to a$, $c_x\to a$, so the derivative-ratio limit passes to the original quotient.

supplementalBlocks.verification: This proves the endpoint $0/0$ case; an $\infty/\infty$ case needs a separate argument rather than setting infinite endpoint values.

supplementalBlocks.title: A one-sided $\infty/\infty$ version (imported)
supplementalBlocks.statement: If $|f(x)|,|g(x)|\to\infty$ and $f'(x)/g'(x)\to L$ for finite $L$, then $f(x)/g(x)\to L$ under the listed conditions.
hypotheses: $f,g$ are differentiable on a one-sided interval approaching the endpoint.
The derivative ratio tends to a finite $L$.
prerequisites: Cauchy’s mean value theorem plus a fixed interior comparison point

supplementalBlocks.title: Convert a product before using the rule
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Identify the indeterminate form, rewrite as a quotient, then check the new quotient.

steps.label: Form
steps.text: $x\to0^+$ and $\ln x\to-\infty$, so the original expression is a product, not an eligible quotient.

steps.label: Convert
steps.text: $x\ln x=\ln x/(1/x)$ has magnitude $\infty /\infty$; both functions are differentiable for $x>0$, and the denominator derivative is nonzero.

steps.label: Derivative ratio
steps.text: The ratio of derivatives tends to zero.

supplementalBlocks.verification: The quotient rule here concerns limits of ratios, not equality between the original quotient and its derivative quotient at each $x$.

exercises.outcome: Classify eligible, convertible, and ineligible expressions before applying L’Hôpital’s rule.
exercises.prompt: As $x\to0^+$, classify $(e^x-1)/x$, $x^x$, and $(x+1)/x$ as directly eligible, convertible, or ineligible for $L$’$H$ôpital. Evaluate $x^x$ using a justified conversion.
exercises.hint: Take a logarithm of the positive power, then rewrite $x\ln x$ as a quotient.
exercises.solution: $(e^x-1)/x$ is direct $0/0$. The positive power $x^x$ is $0^0$ and first requires $\ln(x^x)=x\ln x=\ln x/(1/x)$, an $\infty/\infty$ quotient. Its derivative ratio is $-x\to0$, so $\ln(x^x)\to0$ and $x^x\to1$. $(x+1)/x$ has numerator approaching 1 and denominator approaching 0, so neither rule applies; it diverges to $+\infty$ from the right.
rubric: Check the form of each original expression.
Use logarithms only for the positive power.
Check differentiability and nonzero denominator derivative after conversion.
Reject the ineligible nonindeterminate quotient.

sections.title: State a usable version
sections.text: For a $0/0$ quotient near a, assume $f$,$g$ are differentiable on a punctured one-sided interval, $g$ and $g'$ are nonzero there, both $f$ and $g$ tend to zero, and $f'$/$g'$ tends to $L$ (finite or infinite). Then $f/g$ tends to $L$. An $\infty/\infty$ version has its own hypotheses. The justification imports Cauchy’s mean value theorem, a two-function extension of MVT.

sections.title: Normalize before applying
sections.text: A product $x\ln x$ as $x\to0^+$ is not itself a quotient. Rewrite it as $\ln x/(1/x)$, an $\infty/\infty$ form. Differentiating numerator and denominator gives $(1/x)/(-1/x^2)=-x\to0$. By contrast, differentiating numerator and denominator of $(x+1)/x$ near zero without checking form would incorrectly discard its infinite behavior.

exercise.prompt: Find $\lim_{x\to0}(e^x-1-x)/x^2$, checking the form at each step.
exercise.hint: The first derivative quotient is $(e^x-1)/(2x)$.
exercise.solution: Initially both numerator and denominator tend to zero. After one application they still do. The second derivative quotient is $e^{x}/2\to 1/2$. Derivatives of the denominators are nonzero on each punctured side, so the limit is $1/2$.
rubric: Verify $0/0$ at both applications.
Use the rule on each side and match the results.

sections.title: An indefinite integral is a family
sections.text: The notation $\int f(x)dx$ denotes antiderivatives $F(x)+C$ on an interval. It is not a signed area with unspecified endpoints. Differentiate a candidate to verify it, and handle disconnected domains separately.

sections.title: Reverse a chain rule carefully
sections.text: For $\int 2x \cos(x^{2})dx$, notice that 2x is the derivative of the inner $x^{2}$. The answer is $\sin(x^{2})+C$. Omitting 2x would produce a different problem; there is no general rule integrating a composition by simply integrating the outer function.

exercise.prompt: Find $\int(3x^2-4x+2)\,dx$ and verify it.
exercise.hint: Integrate each power, then differentiate.
exercise.solution: $x^{3}-2x^{2}+2x+C$ differentiates to $3x^{2}-4x+2$. Every antiderivative on $\mathbb{R}$ differs by one constant.
rubric: Include the constant.
Use differentiation as an independent check.

sections.title: A partition is more than equal bars
sections.text: Partition $[a,b]$ into subintervals, choose a tag in each, and sum $f(tag)$ times width. Riemann integrability means all such sums approach one number as the largest width tends to zero, independently of tags. Continuous functions on a closed interval are integrable; this result uses uniform continuity.

sections.title: Signed accumulation
sections.text: For $f(x)=x$ on $[-1,1]$, negative left-hand contributions cancel positive right-hand contributions, giving integral zero. The geometric area is instead $\int |x|dx=1$. Increasing equal bars supplies evidence but is not the definition’s all-partition proof.

exercise.prompt: Compute right-endpoint sums for $x$ on $[0,1]$ and their limit.
exercise.hint: Use width $1/n$ and $\sum k=n(n+1)/2$.
exercise.solution: The sum is $\sum (k/n)(1/n)=(n+1)/(2n)$, tending to $1/2$. Continuity independently ensures this limit equals the Riemann integral.
rubric: Include the subinterval width.
Distinguish one sequence of sums from the full integrability theorem.

sections.title: Average height
sections.text: On $[a,b]$ with $a<b$, the integral average is $(b-a)^{-1}\int f$. It is the constant height producing the same signed accumulation. For a continuous function, an integral mean-value theorem ensures some $c$ has $f(c)$ equal to that average.

sections.title: Attainment needs care
sections.text: For $f=x^{2}$ on $[0,2]$, the integral is $8/3$ and average $4/3$, attained at $c=2/\sqrt{3}$. A discontinuous function taking only values 0 and 1 can have average $1/2$ without ever taking that value.

exercise.prompt: Find the average of $2x+1$ on $[1,3]$ and where it is attained.
exercise.hint: Divide the integral by interval length 2.
exercise.solution: The integral $[x^{2}+x]_{1}^{3}$ is 10, so the average is 5. Solve $2c+1=5$ to get $c=2$.
rubric: Divide by length, not the upper endpoint.
Separate the average from the point attaining it.

sections.title: Two directions, two jobs
sections.text: If $f$ is continuous and $A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$, then $A'(x)=f(x)$. If $F'=f$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a)$. The first constructs an antiderivative; the second evaluates accumulation using one.

sections.title: Moving bounds
sections.text: For $H(x)=\int_x^{x^2}\sin t\,dt$, write $A(x^{2})-A(x)$. Chain rule gives $H'(x)=2x\sin(x^2)-\sin x$. The symbol $t$ is a dummy variable; the moving endpoint $x^{2}$ creates its own derivative factor.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $\int_0^{x^3}e^{t^2}\,dt$.
exercise.hint: Use FTC at the endpoint, then multiply by its derivative.
exercise.solution: The derivative is $3x^{2} e^{x^6}$. No elementary antiderivative of $e^{t^2}$ is needed.
rubric: Substitute the endpoint into the integrand.
Multiply by $3x^{2}$.

sections.title: Transform the whole integral
sections.text: For $\int_0^1 2xe^{x^2}\,dx$, choose $u=x^{2}$ and $du=2x$ dx. Bounds become 0 and 1, yielding $\int_0^1e^u\,du=e-1$. In an indefinite integral substitute back; in a definite integral either transform bounds or return to the original variable before evaluating.

sections.title: Why the rule holds
sections.text: If $F'=f$, then $(F(g(x)))'=f(g(x))g'(x)$. FTC therefore gives the substitution formula when the differentiability and continuity assumptions hold. Monotonicity simplifies interpretation of transformed regions, but the signed one-variable identity with $g'$ can also cover paths that reverse direction.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate $\int_0^2x\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx$.
exercise.hint: Use $u=1+x^{2}$; the extra factor is $du/2$.
exercise.solution: The bounds become 1 and 5. The integral is $(1/2)\int_1^5u^{1/2}\,du =(5\sqrt{5}-1)/3$.
rubric: Transform both endpoints.
Keep the factor $1/2$.

sections.title: Every bad endpoint gets a limit
sections.text: For $\int_1^\infty x^{-2}\,dx$, define lim $R\to \infty \int_1^R x^{-2}\,dx =\lim(1-1/R)=1$. For an interior singularity $c$, split the interval at $c$ and require both one-sided integrals to converge separately.

sections.title: Cancellation cannot rescue divergence
sections.text: The symmetric integrals of $1/x$ on $[-1,-\varepsilon ]$ and $[\varepsilon ,1]$ cancel, but the negative and positive parts diverge separately. Their symmetric principal value zero is a different notion, not convergence of the improper integral.

exercise.prompt: Does $\int_0^1x^{-3/2}\,dx$ converge?
exercise.hint: Replace the lower endpoint by $\varepsilon >0$.
exercise.solution: The integral from $\varepsilon$ to 1 is $2/\sqrt{\varepsilon }-2$, tending to $+\infty$. It diverges.
rubric: Write the limiting definition.
Check the sign of the antiderivative.
Distinguish divergence from a finite numerical cutoff.

sections.title: Decide the order on each piece
sections.text: Area between $f$ and $g$ over $[a,b]$ is $\int |f-g|$. Solve their intersections and split wherever their order changes. For $x$ and $x^{2}$ on $[0,1]$, $x\geq x^{2}$ and the area is $\int_0^1(x-x^2)\,dx=1/6$.

sections.title: Horizontal slices are an alternative
sections.text: A horizontal slice contributes right boundary minus left boundary times dy. For $x=y^{2}$ and $x=2-y^{2}$, intersections occur at $y=\pm 1$; the area is $\int_{-1}^1(2-2y^2)\,dy=8/3$. Choose an order that avoids unnecessary inverses and splitting.

exercise.prompt: Find the area between $y=x$ and $y=-x$ on $[-1,1]$.
exercise.hint: Their order switches at zero.
exercise.solution: Area is $\int_{-1}^0(-2x)\,dx+\int_0^1 2x\,dx=2$. The unsplit signed integral of 2x is zero and is not the area.
rubric: Locate the order change.
Use nonnegative slice heights.

sections.title: A washer removes an inner disk
sections.text: Rotating $y=x$ and $y=x^{2}$ for $0\leq x\leq 1$ about the $x$-axis gives $R=x$ and $r=x^{2}$, so $V=\pi\int_0^1(x^2-x^4)\,dx =2\pi /15$. The slice area is $\pi (R^{2}-r^{2})$, not $\pi (R-r)^{2}$.

sections.title: Measure from the actual axis
sections.text: About $y=-1$ the same region has radii $1+x$ and $1+x^{2}$. The volume becomes $\pi\int_0^1[(1+x)^2-(1+x^2)^2]\,dx=7\pi /15$. Both radii are distances from the axis, not graph heights above zero.

sections.title: The slice shape determines its area
sections.text: A volume built on the base $0\leq x\leq 1$, $x^{2}\leq y\leq x$ need not come from rotation. If every perpendicular section at $x$ is a square, its side is $x-x^{2}$ and area is $(x-x^{2})^{2}$. Thus $V=\int _{0}^{1}(x-x^{2})^{2}dx=1/30$. For an equilateral triangle with that side, multiply the squared side by $\sqrt{3}/4$. A disk or washer factor $\pi$ belongs only to circular slices.

exercise.prompt: Over the base $0\le x\le1$, $x^2\le y\le x$, a solid has perpendicular cross-sections that are equilateral triangles. Find its volume and explain why no washer radius is needed.
exercise.hint: The triangle side is the vertical width $x-x^{2}$; its area is $\sqrt{3}$ times side squared divided by 4.
exercise.solution: $A(x)=\sqrt{3}(x-x^{2})^{2}/4$. Since $\int _{0}^{1}(x-x^{2})^{2}dx=1/30$, $V=\sqrt{3}/120$. The solid is specified by triangular sections, not by rotating the base region.
rubric: Use the actual section shape and vertical base width.
Square the width before integrating over $x$.
Do not insert a circular $\pi$ factor.

sections.title: Unroll a thin shell
sections.text: A shell at radius $r$, height $h$ and thickness dr has volume approximately circumference times height times thickness, $2\pi rh$ dr. Integrating gives the limit. For the region under $y=x$ on $[0,1]$ about the $y$-axis, $V=2\pi\int_0^1x^2\,dx =2\pi /3$.

sections.title: Choose slices relative to the axis
sections.text: Shell slices are parallel to the rotation axis; washer slices are perpendicular. Radii are nonnegative distances. If the region crosses the axis, naive shells from both sides may sweep the same volume twice; first describe the actual solid or split without overlap.

sections.title: Hold the region and axis fixed when comparing methods
sections.text: For the SAME region $0\leq x\leq 1$, $x^{2}\leq y\leq x$ rotated about the $x$-axis, vertical washers use outer radius $x$ and inner radius $x^{2}$: $\pi \int _{0}^{1}(x^{2}-x^{4})dx=2\pi /15$. Horizontal shells use radius $y$ and height $\sqrt{y}-y$: $2\pi \int _{0}^{1}y(\sqrt{y}-y)dy=2\pi /15$. The inversion $x=y$ or $x=\sqrt{y}$ comes from that same region; changing the axis would compare different solids.

exercise.prompt: For the fixed region $0\le x\le1$, $0\le y\le1-x$ rotated about the $y$-axis, set up both shells and perpendicular disks, and verify the same volume.
exercise.hint: Vertical shells have radius $x$ and height $1-x$. Horizontal disks have radius $1-y$.
exercise.solution: Shells give $2\pi \int _{0}^{1}x(1-x)dx=\pi /3$. Disks give $\pi \int _{0}^{1}(1-y)^{2}dy=\pi /3$. Both descriptions use the same triangle and $y$-axis, and neither double-counts the solid.
rubric: Keep the same region and $y$-axis in both setups.
Identify shell radius and height and disk radius with the correct variables.
Evaluate and reconcile both integrals.

sections.title: Repeated and cyclic parts
sections.text: From $(uv)'=u'v+uv'$, $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$. Repeated parts gives $\int x^{2}e^{x}dx=e^{x}(x^{2}-2x+2)+C$. For $I=\int e^x\cos x\,dx$, two rounds give $I=e^{x}\cos x+e^{x}\sin x-I$; solving yields $I=e^{x}(\sin x+\cos x)/2+C$.

sections.title: Definite terms and choice
sections.text: For $\int_0^1xe^x\,dx$, choose $u=x$, $dv=e^{x}dx$. The boundary term $[xe^{x}]_{0}^{1}=e$ and the remaining integral is $e-1$, so the answer is 1. Choosing $u=e^{x}$ and $dv=x$ dx creates an $x^{2}e^{x}$ integral, increasing the polynomial degree instead of reducing it.

sections.title: Stage the next method after parts
sections.text: For $\int x \arctan$ $x$ dx, choose $u=\arctan$ $x$ and $dv=x$ dx because differentiating the inverse tangent gives a rational function. Parts yields $x^{2}$ arctan $x/2-(1/2)\int x^{2}/(1+x^{2})dx$. Divide $x^{2}/(1+x^{2})=1-1/(1+x^{2})$, then finish with $x^{2}$ arctan $x/2-x/2+\arctan x/2+C$. The second method is chosen after seeing the simpler remainder.

exercise.prompt: Choose and justify the first method for $\int_0^1 x\arctan x\,dx$, then identify the second method needed for the remainder and evaluate.
exercise.hint: Let $u=\arctan$ $x$ and $dv=x$ dx. After parts, divide $x^{2}$ by $1+x^{2}$ before integrating.
exercise.solution: Parts is useful because $d(\arctan x)=dx/(1+x^2)$. It gives $[x^2\arctan x/2]_0^1-(1/2)\int_0^1x^2/(1+x^2)\,dx$. Divide $x^2/(1+x^2)=1-1/(1+x^2)$; the result is $\pi/4-1/2$. Choosing $u=x$ makes the antiderivative of $\arctan x$ the harder first step.
rubric: Justify the $u$,dv choice before calculating.
Use rational division for the remainder.
Apply both endpoint terms and simplify.

sections.title: Use parity to choose a substitution
sections.text: For $\sin^m x\cos^n x$ with a positive odd sine power, reserve $\sin x\,dx$ and replace $\sin^2x$ by $1-\cos^2x$; then use $u=\cos x$. With an odd cosine power, reverse the roles. If both powers are even, use half-angle identities.

sections.title: Work both branches
sections.text: $\int\sin^3x\cos^2x\,dx$ becomes $-\int(1-u^2)u^2\,du=-u^3/3+u^5/5+C$. For $\int\cos^2x\,dx$, use $\cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2$, giving $x/2+\sin2x/4+C$.

exercise.prompt: Find $\int\sin x\cos^3x\,dx$.
exercise.hint: Reserve $\sin x\,dx$ and use $u=\cos x$.
exercise.solution: The integral is $-\int u^3\,du=-\cos^4x/4+C$. Differentiating restores $\sin x\cos^3x$.
rubric: Carry the minus sign in du.
Verify by differentiating.

sections.title: Fix a branch before simplifying
sections.text: For $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ with $a>0$, choose $x=a\sin\theta$ and $\theta\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$, so $\cos\theta\ge0$ and $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}=a\cos\theta$. Without the range restriction the root is $a|\cos\theta|$. For $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$, $x=a\tan\theta$ on the same open angle interval gives $a\sec\theta$.

sections.title: Include the differential
sections.text: For $\int\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$, $x=\sin\theta$ and $dx=\cos\theta\,d\theta$ give $\int\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$. Substituting back gives $(\arcsin x+x\sqrt{1-x^2})/2+C$ on the interior of $[-1,1]$. A diagram helps recover the factors but does not replace the branch choice.

sections.title: The secant branch depends on the x-domain
sections.text: For $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$, $a>0$ and $x\ge a$, take $x=a\sec\theta$ with $0\le\theta<\pi/2$. Then $\tan\theta\ge0$ and $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}=a\tan\theta$, not $a|\tan\theta|$. On $x\le-a$ use $x=-a\sec\theta$ on the same angle range and transform $dx$ with its negative sign. One substitution formula cannot silently cross the gap $(-a,a)$.

sections.title: The tangent branch keeps secant positive
sections.text: For $\sqrt{x^2+4}$, $x=2\tan\theta$ with $-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2$ gives $\sec\theta>0$, so $\sqrt{x^2+4}=2\sec\theta$. In $\int dx/(x^2+4)^{3/2}$, $dx=2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ reduces the integrand to $\cos\theta/4$. The result is $x/[4\sqrt{x^2+4}]+C$. Without the angle range, replacing $\sqrt{\sec^2\theta}$ by $\sec\theta$ could have the wrong sign.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate $A=\int_2^4 dx/\sqrt{x^2-4}$ and $B=\int_0^3 dx/(x^2+9)^{3/2}$ by trigonometric substitutions. Choose secant or tangent for each, state the branches, and transform the bounds.
exercise.hint: For A use $x=2sec \theta$, $0\leq \theta \leq \pi /3$. For $B$ use $x=3tan \theta$, $0\leq \theta \leq \pi /4$. Check the sign of each square root on its chosen branch.
exercise.solution: A: $x=2\sec\theta$ gives $\sqrt{x^2-4}=2\tan\theta$ and $dx=2\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta$ on $0\le\theta\le\pi/3$, so $A=\int_0^{\pi/3}\sec\theta\,d\theta=\ln(2+\sqrt3)$. $B$: $x=3\tan\theta$ gives $\sqrt{x^2+9}=3\sec\theta>0$ and $dx=3\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ on $0\le\theta\le\pi/4$, so $B=(1/9)\int_0^{\pi/4}\cos\theta\,d\theta=\sqrt2/18$. Both signs follow from the declared branches.
rubric: Choose secant for the difference and tangent for the sum, with explicit branches.
Transform bounds, differentials, and square-root signs for both.
Evaluate both transformed integrals.

supplementalBlocks.title: Divide before decomposing an improper fraction
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Compare degrees before choosing partial-fraction terms; decompose only the proper remainder.
supplementalBlocks.setup: For the notes' example, integrate $R(x)=(x^4-2x^2+4x+1)/(x^3-x^2-x+1)$ on an interval avoiding $x=-1,1$.

steps.label: Divide
steps.text: Since the numerator has degree four and the denominator degree three, long division gives $R(x)=x+1+4x/(x^3-x^2-x+1)$.

steps.label: Factor and choose terms
steps.text: $x^3-x^2-x+1=(x-1)^2(x+1)$, so the proper remainder needs $A/(x-1)+B/(x-1)^2+C/(x+1)$. Solving $4x=A(x-1)(x+1)+B(x+1)+C(x-1)^2$ gives $(A,B,C)=(1,2,-1)$.

steps.label: Integrate on a domain component
steps.text: $\int R(x)\,dx=x^2/2+x+\ln|x-1|-2/(x-1)-\ln|x+1|+C$. The constant may differ on $(-\infty,-1)$, $(-1,1)$, and $(1,\infty)$.

supplementalBlocks.result: Division precedes the repeated-factor template whenever the original rational function is improper.
supplementalBlocks.verification: Differentiate the result on any component and recover $x+1+1/(x-1)+2/(x-1)^2-1/(x+1)=R(x)$.

exercises.outcome: Choose polynomial division before repeated-factor decomposition for an improper rational integrand.
exercises.prompt: Integrate $\int (x^4-3x^2-3x-7)/[(x+1)^2(x-2)]\,dx$ on an interval where it is defined. State why division comes first, include every repeated-factor term, and verify by differentiation.
exercises.hint: The numerator degree exceeds the denominator degree. Division gives quotient $x$ and remainder $-x-7$; write $A/(x+1)+B/(x+1)^2+C/(x-2)$ for the proper part.
exercises.solution: The denominator is $x^3-3x-2$, so division gives $x+(-x-7)/[(x+1)^2(x-2)]$. Multiplying the template through and solving gives $(A,B,C)=(1,2,-1)$. Hence the integrand is $x+1/(x+1)+2/(x+1)^2-1/(x-2)$ and the antiderivative is $x^2/2+\ln|x+1|-2/(x+1)-\ln|x-2|+C$ on each component of $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1,2\}$. Differentiation recovers the decomposition and original quotient.
rubric: Compare polynomial degrees and divide before decomposing.
Include both powers of the repeated factor and solve the coefficient identity.
Integrate on a domain component and check the derivative.

sections.title: The denominator determines the template
sections.text: First divide if numerator degree is at least denominator degree. For each repeated linear factor $(x-a)^k$ include $A_{1}/(x-a)+…+A_{k}/(x-a)^k$. For an irreducible quadratic $q$, use a linear numerator $(Bx+C)/q$; repeat terms for powers of $q$.

sections.title: Solve coefficients explicitly
sections.text: For $(x^{2}+1)/(x(x-1)^{2})$, write $A/x+B/(x-1)+C/(x-1)^{2}$. Multiplying through gives $x^{2}+1=A(x-1)^{2}+Bx(x-1)+Cx$. Setting $x=0$ gives $A=1$, $x=1$ gives $C=2$, and the $x^{2}$ coefficient gives $B=0$. Integrating yields $\ln|x|-2/(x-1)+C_{0}$ on each component. For $(x+1)/(x^{2}+1)$, split into a logarithmic derivative and an arctangent: $(1/2)\ln(x^{2}+1)+\arctan$ $x$.

sections.title: Decide the algebra before integrating
sections.text: For a rational integrand, first compare polynomial degrees and divide if improper. Factor the remaining denominator over the reals, then include every power of a repeated linear factor and a linear numerator over each irreducible quadratic. Solve the coefficient identity and only then integrate. This algebraic route differs from parts, which is chosen for a product whose differentiated factor simplifies. Verify a proposed antiderivative by differentiation on each domain component.

exercise.prompt: Choose the first algebraic step, then integrate $\int(2x+3)/[x(x+1)^2]\,dx$ on one interval avoiding its poles. Explain why a repeated-factor term is required.
exercise.hint: The rational function is proper. Write $A/x+B/(x+1)+C/(x+1)^{2}$ before solving coefficients.
exercise.solution: No division is needed. The repeated factor requires both $1/(x+1)$ and $1/(x+1)^{2}$ terms. Solving $2x+3=A(x+1)^{2}+Bx(x+1)+Cx$ gives $A=3$, $B=-3$, $C=-1$. Integrating gives $3\ln|x|-3\ln|x+1|+1/(x+1)+C$ on each interval separated by $-1$ and 0.
rubric: Check properness and factor structure before choosing the template.
Include both powers of the repeated factor and solve the identity.
Integrate with logarithm signs and domain components intact.

sections.title: Signed errors reveal geometry
sections.text: For a convex function, chords lie above the graph, so the trapezoidal rule overestimates; midpoint underestimates when convexity holds on each panel. Error signs require hypotheses, not just a visual impression.

sections.title: Choose n from a bound
sections.text: For a twice continuously differentiable function with $|f''|\leq M$, composite midpoint error is at most $M(b-a)^{3}/(24n^{2})$, and trapezoidal error at most $M(b-a)^{3}/(12n^{2})$. Solve the inequality for $n$ and round up; these are certified bounds, unlike agreement between two numerical estimates.

exercise.prompt: How many trapezoids guarantee error at most 0.001 for $\int_0^1x^2\,dx$?
exercise.hint: Here $M=2$; require $2/(12n^{2})\leq 0.001$.
exercise.solution: $n^{2}\geq 500/3$, so $n\geq 13$ is sufficient. The bound is $1/(6\cdot 169)$, below 0.001.
rubric: Use an upper derivative bound on the whole interval.
Round $n$ upward.

sections.title: Pairs of panels
sections.text: Composite Simpson requires an even number $n$ of equal subintervals with width $h$. Its weights are 1,4,2,4,…,2,4,1 and overall factor $h/3$. It integrates every polynomial of degree at most three exactly, although each local interpolant is quadratic.

sections.title: A fourth-derivative guarantee
sections.text: If $f$ has a continuous fourth derivative bounded in magnitude by $M$, the error is at most $M(b-a)^{5}/(180n^{4})$. More panels do not make this bound applicable at a singularity; check smoothness first.

exercise.prompt: Apply Simpson with $n=2$ to $x^3$ on $[0,1]$.
exercise.hint: Use values at 0, $1/2$ and 1.
exercise.solution: With $h=1/2$, the result is $(1/6)[0+4(1/8)+1]=1/4$, exactly the integral.
rubric: Use the $h/3$ factor.
Explain exactness for a cubic.

sections.title: The input is an index
sections.text: A sequence converges to $L$ if for every $\varepsilon >0$ some integer $N$ makes $|a_{n}-L|<\varepsilon$ for every $n\geq N$. The tail matters: changing finitely many terms cannot change the limit. An infinite sequence does not automatically converge.

sections.title: A quantitative tail
sections.text: For $a_{n}=1+1/n$, $|a_{n}-1|=1/n$. Choose an integer $N>1/\varepsilon$; then all $n\geq N$ satisfy the required inequality. A plot of the first hundred values cannot alone establish an assertion about every later term.

exercise.prompt: Give an $N$ ensuring $|(2+3/n)-2|<0.01$ for every $n\ge N$.
exercise.hint: Solve $3/n<0.01$ with a strict inequality.
exercise.solution: Any integer $N\geq 301$ works. $N=300$ fails at its first term because the error equals 0.01.
rubric: Respect strict inequality.
Make a statement about all later indices.

sections.title: Subsequences inherit a genuine limit
sections.text: A subsequence selects indices $n_{1}<n_{2}<…$ tending to infinity. If $a_{n}\to L$, every subsequence tends to $L$. Hence two subsequences with distinct limits refute convergence. For $(-1)^n$, the even and odd subsequences tend to 1 and $-1$.

sections.title: Bounded does not mean convergent
sections.text: Every convergent real sequence is bounded, but $(-1)^n$ is a bounded counterexample to the converse. Bolzano–Weierstrass states that every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence. It does not say the whole sequence converges.

exercise.prompt: Does $a_n=(-1)^n+1/n$ converge?
exercise.hint: Separate even and odd indices.
exercise.solution: The even subsequence tends to 1 and the odd subsequence to $-1$. Therefore the sequence diverges while remaining bounded.
rubric: Use subsequences whose indices tend to infinity.
Distinguish boundedness from convergence.

sections.title: Normalize polynomial growth
sections.text: For $(3n^{2}+n)/(2n^{2}-1)$, divide by $n^{2}$ to obtain $(3+1/n)/(2-1/n^{2})$, whose limit is $3/2$. The denominator limit 2 is nonzero, allowing the quotient law.

sections.title: A zero denominator gives no automatic result
sections.text: The sequences $1/n$ and $1/n^{2}$ both tend to zero, but their quotient is $n$ and diverges. Reversing them gives $1/n\to 0$. Equal component limits therefore do not settle an indeterminate quotient.

exercise.prompt: Find $\lim_{n\to\infty}(\sqrt{n^2+n}-n)$.
exercise.hint: Rationalize before taking limits.
exercise.solution: The expression equals $n/(\sqrt{n^{2}+n}+n)=1/(\sqrt{1+1/n}+1)$, tending to $1/2$.
rubric: Avoid subtracting two divergent limits.
Use a valid algebraic identity for positive $n$.

sections.title: Prove bounds for a recurrence
sections.text: Let $a_{1}=1$ and $a_{n+1}=\sqrt{2+a_{n}}$. If $1\leq a_{n}\leq 2$, then $1\leq a_{n+1}\leq 2$; induction bounds every term. On $[1,2]$, $\sqrt{2+x}\geq x$ because $2+x-x^{2}=(2-x)(x+1)\geq 0$, so the sequence is increasing.

sections.title: Only now solve the fixed point
sections.text: An increasing bounded real sequence converges by completeness. Taking limits gives $L=\sqrt{2+L}$, hence $L=2$ or $-1$ after squaring. The proven bounds force $L=2$. Solving the equation before proving convergence would produce candidates without showing that the sequence approaches any of them.

exercise.prompt: Let $b_1=3$ and $b_{n+1}=(b_n+2)/2$. Prove convergence and find the limit.
exercise.hint: Show $b_{n}\geq 2$ and $b_{n+1}\leq b_{n}$ by induction.
exercise.solution: The recurrence preserves $b_{n}\geq 2$, and $b_{n+1}-b_{n}=(2-b_{n})/2\leq 0$. Thus it converges. Its limit satisfies $L=(L+2)/2$, giving $L=2$; explicitly $b_{n}=2+2^{1-n}$.
rubric: Prove both boundedness and monotonicity.
Invoke convergence before passing the limit through the recurrence.

sections.title: Sum means a limit of partial sums
sections.text: For a series starting at $n=0$, define $S_{N}$ as its first $N$ terms, from $n=0$ through $n=N-1$. Convergence means $S_{N}$ approaches a finite number, not merely $a_{n}\to 0$.
