For the geometric series, $S_N=1+r+\cdots+r^{N-1}=(1-r^N)/(1-r)$ when $r\ne 1$; at $N=1$ this is just 1. Its infinite sum is $1/(1-r)$ only for $|r|<1$. Some books instead use $S_{N}$ for the sum through index $N$; that has $N+1$ terms and numerator $1-r^{N+1}$.

sections.title: Keep the surviving boundary terms
sections.text: For $\sum_{n=1}^\infty1/[n(n+1)]$, split each term into $1/n-1/(n+1)$. The $N$th partial sum is $1-1/(N+1)$, tending to $1$. Writing the finite cancellation first prevents informal infinity-minus-infinity errors.

exercise.prompt: Find $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(1/3)^n$.
exercise.hint: Identify the first term, not just the ratio.
exercise.solution: The first term is $1/9$ and ratio $1/3$, so the sum is $(1/9)/(1-1/3)=1/6$.
rubric: Use the correct starting index.
Check the ratio magnitude.

sections.title: Necessary is not sufficient
sections.text: If partial sums converge, then $a_{n}=S_{n}-S_{n-1}\to 0$. Thus failure of $a_{n}\to 0$ proves divergence. A zero term limit is inconclusive: $\sum 1/n$ diverges, whereas $\sum 1/n^{2}$ converges.

sections.title: A harmonic-series proof
sections.text: Group terms from $2^{k-1}+1$ to $2^k$. There are $2^{k-1}$ terms, each at least $1/2^k$, so each group contributes at least $1/2$. Arbitrarily many groups force partial sums to grow without bound, despite individual terms tending to zero.

exercise.prompt: What does the term test say about $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n/(n+1)$ and $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^2$?
exercise.hint: Compute the term limits and distinguish a verdict from inconclusiveness.
exercise.solution: The first term limit is 1, so its series diverges. The second term limit is zero, so this test alone gives no verdict; a $p$-series or integral argument proves convergence.
rubric: Use the test only to rule out convergence.
Do not call the second result a proof of convergence.

sections.title: A comparison of positive tails
sections.text: If $f$ is positive, continuous and decreasing eventually, with $a_n=f(n)$, then $\sum a_n$ and $\int f$ share convergence behavior. Finite initial exceptions do not affect convergence. This is not an equality between sum and integral.

sections.title: A logarithmic benchmark
sections.text: For $n\geq 2$, compare $\sum 1/[n(\log n)^p]$ with $\int_2^\infty dx/[x(\log x)^p]$. Positivity and eventual decrease hold for every fixed real $p$. Substituting $u=\log x$ gives $\int_{\log 2}^{\infty}u^{-p}\,du$: it converges exactly when $p>1$. The boundary $p=1$ diverges, despite the extra logarithm. This benchmark is useful when a plain $p$-series comparison loses the decisive $\log$ factor.

sections.title: Bound the remainder
sections.text: For a convergent positive decreasing series, $\int_{N+1}^\infty f(x)\,dx\le\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty a_n\le\int_N^\infty f(x)\,dx$. For $a_n=1/n^2$ this gives $1/(N+1)\le R_N\le1/N$, a usable accuracy guarantee.

exercise.prompt: How large must $N$ be to guarantee remainder at most $0.001$ for $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^2$?
exercise.hint: Use the upper integral bound $1/N$.
exercise.solution: $N\geq 1000$ suffices, since $R_N\leq 1/N\leq 0.001$. The bound is conservative and does not claim equality.
rubric: Use the upper bound for a guarantee.
State the positive decreasing hypothesis.

sections.title: Match the inequality to the conclusion
sections.text: For nonnegative terms, $a_n\le b_n$ and convergence of $\sum b_n$ imply convergence of $\sum a_n$. If $a_n\ge b_n$ and $\sum b_n$ diverges, $\sum a_n$ diverges. Reversing these directions gives no conclusion.

sections.title: Limit comparison
sections.text: For positive $a_n,b_n$, if $a_{n}/b_{n}\to L$ with $0<L<\infty$, the series share behavior. For $a_{n}=1/(n^{2}+n)$, use $b_{n}=1/n^{2}$: their ratio $n/(n+1)\to 1$, so the series converges. Ratio zero or infinity requires a one-sided argument rather than the same equivalence.

exercise.prompt: Decide whether $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/\sqrt{n^2+1}$ converges.
exercise.hint: Compare to $1/n$ and compute the ratio.
exercise.solution: The ratio $n/\sqrt{n^{2}+1}=1/\sqrt{1+1/n^{2}}$ tends to 1. The harmonic series diverges, so this positive series diverges.
rubric: Choose the dominant-power comparison.
Verify a finite strictly positive ratio.

contentBlocks.title: Alternating Series Test (imported)
contentBlocks.statement: If $b_n>0$ decreases to $0$, then $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}b_n$ converges. This alone does not decide absolute convergence.
hypotheses: The signs alternate and the magnitudes $b_n$ are eventually nonincreasing and tend to $0$.

contentBlocks.title: Convergence and absolute convergence are separate
contentBlocks.strategy: First establish the signed series using the alternating test, then test its magnitudes with a positive-series benchmark.
contentBlocks.setup: Classify $S=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}/\sqrt n$, the example on MH1101 Chapter 05 Notes physical page 17.

steps.label: Check the alternating hypotheses
steps.text: The positive magnitudes $b_n=1/\sqrt n$ decrease and tend to $0$, so the Alternating Series Test proves convergence of $S$.

steps.label: Test absolute convergence separately
steps.text: Taking absolute values removes the signs and produces a $p$-series with $p=1/2\le1$, which diverges.

contentBlocks.result: $S$ is conditionally convergent: the signed sum converges, but its absolute-value series diverges.
contentBlocks.verification: The fact that $b_n\to0$ is necessary but does not by itself prove convergence; the decrease and alternating signs supply the signed-series verdict.

sections.title: Separate two convergence questions
sections.text: Absolute convergence means $\sum|a_n|$ converges and implies convergence of $\sum a_n$. Conditional convergence means $\sum a_n$ converges but $\sum|a_n|$ diverges. The alternating harmonic series is conditional: its magnitudes decrease to zero, but their harmonic sum diverges.

sections.title: Alternating remainder
sections.text: If positive magnitudes decrease to zero, the error after $N$ alternating terms has magnitude at most the next term and its sign matches the next term. For $\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^{n+1}/n$, the error is at most $1/(N+1)$. Without eventual decrease, this bound needs another justification.

exercise.prompt: Classify $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^n/n^2$.
exercise.hint: Test the absolute-value series first.
exercise.solution: Its absolute-value series $\sum 1/n^{2}$ converges, so the original series converges absolutely. Calling it conditional merely because signs alternate is incorrect.
rubric: Test magnitudes independently.
Use the definition of conditional convergence.

exercises.outcome: Classify a signed alternating series by checking its magnitudes and its absolute-value series separately.
exercises.prompt: Classify $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}n/(n^2+1)$ as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent. Justify both tests you use.
exercises.hint: For $b_n=n/(n^2+1)$, inspect the derivative of $x/(x^2+1)$ on $x\ge1$. Compare the positive series with $\sum 1/n$ by a limit ratio.
exercises.solution: For $x\ge1$, the derivative of $x/(x^2+1)$ is $(1-x^2)/(x^2+1)^2\le0$. Thus $b_n$ decreases to $0$, so the alternating series converges. But $b_n/(1/n)=n^2/(n^2+1)\to1$; limit comparison with the divergent harmonic series shows $\sum b_n$ diverges. The signed series is conditionally convergent.
rubric: Establish positive magnitudes, eventual decrease and zero limit before applying the alternating test.
Test absolute values using a valid positive-series comparison.
State conditional convergence only after both verdicts.

sections.title: Different tests suit different forms
sections.text: For $a_{n}=x^n/n$!, the absolute ratio is $|x|/(n+1)\to 0$, so the series converges for every fixed $x$. For $a_{n}=(n/(2n+1))^n$, the nth-root magnitude tends to $1/2$, giving absolute convergence without expanding a complicated neighboring-term ratio.

sections.title: A limit of one is inconclusive
sections.text: Both $1/n$ and $1/n^{2}$ have ratio and nth-root limits equal to 1, yet one series diverges and the other converges. For ratio or root limit below 1, conclude absolute convergence; above 1, terms fail to tend to zero. More general limsup forms need their own statement.

sections.title: Choose the test from the term's structure
sections.text: Before calculating a limit, ask what conclusion is needed. If terms do not approach zero, stop: the series diverges. For nonnegative terms resembling $1/[n(\log n)^p]$, justify the integral test and check its positivity and decrease hypotheses. A factorial often favors the ratio test; a whole expression raised to $n$ favors the root test. An alternating sign calls for separate absolute and signed convergence checks. If a ratio or root limit is 1, switch to a comparison or integral benchmark. For a power series, the ratio or root calculation only finds the open radius; test both endpoints as separate numerical series.

exercise.prompt: Choose a test before calculating for each: $A=\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}1/[n(\log n)^2]$, $B=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n/3^n$, and $C=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(x-2)^n/n$. Classify $A$ and $B$; find $C$'s interval, checking both endpoints.
exercise.hint: A has a logarithmic benchmark, $B$ has an exponential and factorial factors ratio, and $C$ needs a radius followed by two separate endpoint series.
exercise.solution: For A use the integral test: $f(x)=1/[x(\log x)^{2}]$ is positive, continuous and eventually decreasing; $u=\log x$ makes the tail integral finite, so A converges. For $B$ the ratio of successive positive terms tends to $1/3$, so $B$ converges. For $C$ the ratio gives $|x-2|<1$. At $x=1$ the alternating harmonic series converges conditionally; at $x=3$ the harmonic series diverges. Its interval is $[1,3)$. The ratio limit 1 at the endpoints alone proves neither result.
rubric: Justify each test choice from the term structure before computing.
State the integral-test hypotheses for A and the ratio limit for $B$.
Treat $C$'s two endpoints independently and distinguish conditional convergence.

sections.title: Endpoints are separate series
sections.text: For $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x^n/n$, the ratio test gives convergence for $|x|<1$ and divergence for $|x|>1$. At $x=1$ it is harmonic and diverges; at $x=-1$ it is alternating harmonic and converges conditionally. The interval is $[-1,1)$, not an automatically closed radius interval.

sections.title: The center shifts everything
sections.text: For $\sum a_{n}(x-c)^n$, the radius measures distance from $c$. A radius can be zero or infinite. Partial sums are polynomials; their limit is defined only on the convergence set, and may behave differently at its boundary.

exercise.prompt: Find the interval of convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(x-2)^n/(n\,3^n)$.
exercise.hint: Use $|x-2|<3$, then inspect both endpoints.
exercise.solution: The radius is 3 about 2. At $x=-1$ the series is alternating harmonic and converges; at $x=5$ it is harmonic and diverges. The interval is $[-1,5)$.
rubric: Shift the radius interval around the correct center.
Test each endpoint independently.

sections.title: Operate inside the radius
sections.text: A power series may be differentiated or integrated term by term inside its radius, and the new series has the same radius. Endpoint convergence can change. The theorem relies on uniform control on each smaller closed interval and is imported here, rather than proved by formal symbol manipulation.

sections.title: Derive a logarithmic series
sections.text: Integrating $\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n=1/(1-x)$ from $0$ to $x$ gives $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x^n/n=-\ln(1-x)$ for $|x|<1$. The integration constant is fixed by the zero value at $x=0$. At $x=-1$ an additional endpoint argument is needed; interior validity alone does not prove it.

exercise.prompt: Differentiate $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x^n/n$ inside its radius. What happens at $x=-1$?
exercise.hint: The differentiated coefficients lose the factor $1/n$.
exercise.solution: The derivative series is $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x^{n-1}=1/(1-x)$ for $|x|<1$. At $x=-1$ its terms alternate $\pm 1$ and do not tend to zero, so it diverges although the original series converges there.
rubric: State the open interval of termwise validity.
Recheck endpoints after differentiation.

contentBlocks.title: Taylor’s finite remainder theorem (imported)
contentBlocks.statement: For $x$ near $a$, $f(x)=P_n(x)+f^{(n+1)}(\xi)(x-a)^{n+1}/(n+1)!$ for some $\xi$ between $a$ and $x$.
hypotheses: $f$ has $n+1$ continuous derivatives on an interval containing $a$ and $x$.
prerequisites: Mean value theorem and repeated differentiation

sections.title: A polynomial is not automatically an infinite expansion
sections.text: Taylor’s polynomial uses derivatives at one center. Taylor’s theorem supplies a finite remainder under sufficient differentiability; equality with the infinite Taylor series additionally requires that remainder to tend to zero. Smoothness alone does not ensure that.

sections.title: A smooth counterexample
sections.text: Define $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=\exp(-1/x^{2})$ for $x\ne 0$. Every derivative at zero vanishes (exponential decay dominates each inverse power), so its Taylor series is zero, yet $f(x)>0$ away from zero. For $e^x$ on a bounded interval, by contrast, the factorial remainder bound tends to zero.

sections.title: Choose a nonzero center and certify a degree
sections.text: Center $\log x$ at $a=1$: $P_n(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^{k+1}(x-1)^k/k$. For $x=1.2$, $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\leq n!$ on $[1,1.2]$, so Taylor's finite remainder obeys $|R_{n}|\leq0.2^{n+1}/(n+1)$. Degree 2 gives only a 0.00267 guarantee; degree 3 gives $0.0004<0.001$ and $P_{3}(1.2)=0.182666…$. This finite accuracy claim follows from the derivative bound. Equality with an infinite series is a separate limit claim requiring $R_{n}\to 0$.

exercise.prompt: Use a Taylor polynomial centered at $a=1$ to approximate $\log(1.2)$ with certified error below $0.001$. Choose a degree from a remainder bound; state separately what would justify equality with the infinite Taylor series.
exercise.hint: On [1,1.2], |$\frac{d^{n+1}}{dx^{n+1}}\log x|\leq n$!, hence $|R_{n}|\leq0.2^{n+1}/(n+1)$. Compare degrees 2 and 3.
exercise.solution: Degree 3 suffices: $P_{3}(1.2)=0.2-0.2^{2}/2+0.2^{3}/3\approx 0.182667$ and $|R_{3}|\leq 0.2^{4}/4=0.0004$. The degree-2 bound is $0.2^{3}/3\approx 0.00267$, so it does not certify the target. The infinite representation additionally needs proof that $R_{n}\to 0$ (which this bound provides at $x=1.2$)..
rubric: Center at 1 and compute the degree-3 polynomial.
Use a derivative bound to certify the requested error; do not infer it from a decimal approximation.
Separate finite accuracy from equality to the infinite series.

sections.title: Coefficients and termination
sections.text: The coefficient of $x^n$ in $(1+x)^\alpha$ is $\alpha(\alpha-1)\cdots(\alpha-n+1)/n!$, with constant term $1$. For nonnegative integer $\alpha$ the series terminates as a polynomial. Otherwise its expansion is valid for $|x|<1$ and endpoints need separate analysis.

sections.title: A concrete expansion
sections.text: For $\alpha =1/2$ the first terms are $1+x/2-x^{2}/8+x^{3}/16$. This approximates $\sqrt{1+x}$ near zero. For $\alpha =-1$ the coefficients alternate and recover $1/(1+x)=1-x+x^{2}-…$ inside the radius.

exercise.prompt: Find the quadratic Taylor approximation of $(1+x)^{-2}$ at zero.
exercise.hint: Use $\alpha =-2$ in the coefficient formula.
exercise.solution: The first terms are $1-2x+3x^{2}$, with remainder of order $x^{3}$ near zero. The infinite nonterminating series has radius 1.
rubric: Divide the second falling product by 2!.
Do not treat the approximation as exact.

sections.title: Expand far enough to survive cancellation
sections.text: For $(\sin x-x)/x^3$, use $\sin x=x-x^3/6+O(x^5)$. After cancellation and division, the expression is $-1/6+O(x^2)$, so the limit is $-1/6$. Stopping at $\sin x\approx x$ would discard the decisive term.

sections.title: Meaning of error symbols
sections.text: $R(x)=O(x^k)$ means $|R(x)|\le C|x|^k$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood for some fixed $C$. $R(x)=o(x^k)$ means its ratio to $x^k$ tends to zero. Dividing an expansion by $x^m$ also divides its error; retain enough orders to make the resulting error vanish.

exercise.hint: Keep the cubic term and a controlled higher-order remainder.
exercise.solution: Taylor gives numerator $x^{3}/6+O(x^{4})$, so the quotient is $1/6+O(x)$ and tends to $1/6$.
rubric: Retain the first uncancelled term.
Track the remainder after division.

sections.title: Separate points and displacements
sections.text: Points describe locations; their difference is a displacement vector. For $A=(1,-1,2)$, $B=(3,2,2)$, $B-A=(2,3,0)$ has length $\sqrt{13}$. The dot product $u\cdot v=|u||v|\cos \theta$ measures alignment; normalization $v/|v|$ requires $v\ne 0$.

sections.title: Projection is a signed component
sections.text: The scalar component of $v$ along a unit vector $e$ is $v\cdot e$, and the vector projection is $(v\cdot e)e$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|u\cdot v|\leq |u||v|$, the estimate later used for gradient bounds. Orthogonal vectors have dot product zero; the zero vector has no direction.

exercise.prompt: Project $v=(3,4,0)$ onto the direction $(1,1,0)$.
exercise.hint: Normalize the direction first.
exercise.solution: The unit direction is $e=(1,1,0)/\sqrt{2}$. The scalar component is $7/\sqrt{2}$ and vector projection is $(7/2,7/2,0)$. The residual $(-1/2,1/2,0)$ is perpendicular to $e$.
rubric: Normalize a nonzero vector.
Distinguish scalar component from vector projection.
Check the residual dot product.

sections.title: One trace, several clocks
sections.text: The circle $r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$ traces once for $0\le t\le2\pi$ and twice for $0\le t\le4\pi$. The image set is unchanged, but traversal-sensitive integrals count both passes. Reversing $t$ reverses orientation; a positive increasing change of clock preserves it.

sections.title: Speed enters length
sections.text: For $r(t)=(\cos2t,\sin2t)$, speed is $2$. On $[0,\pi]$ the length is $\int_0^\pi2\,dt=2\pi$, one traversal. The unit-speed parameter is arc length, not every parameter called $t$.

exercise.prompt: Compare the lengths of $r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$ on $[0,2\pi]$ and $[0,4\pi]$.
exercise.hint: Length integrates speed over the actual parameter interval.
exercise.solution: The lengths are $2\pi$ and $4\pi$. The geometric image is the same circle, but the second curve traverses it twice.
rubric: Use the interval as part of the parametrized curve.
Do not confuse image length with traversal length.

sections.title: Use the defining constraint
sections.text: A line from $A$ to $B$ is $A+t(B-A)$, $0\le t\le1$. An ellipse $x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2=1$ is $(a\cos t,b\sin t)$. For an intersection with $z=x^2+y^2$, substitute a planar parametrization into $z$ to satisfy both equations.

sections.title: Check coverage and orientation
sections.text: The intersection $x^2+y^2=1$ and $z=x+y$ can be written $(\cos t,\sin t,\cos t+\sin t)$, $0\le t\le2\pi$. It traverses once counterclockwise in $xy$ projection. Substitution verifies membership; the full parameter interval verifies coverage.

exercise.prompt: Parametrize the line segment from $(1,0,2)$ to $(0,3,1)$.
exercise.hint: Add $t$ times the endpoint difference.
exercise.solution: $r(t)=(1-t,3t,2-t)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$. At 0 and 1 it gives the assigned endpoints, with orientation from the first to the second.
rubric: Supply the parameter interval.
Check both endpoints and direction.

sections.title: Regularity belongs to the parametrization
sections.text: A regular curve has nonzero velocity. The map $r(t)=(t^{3},0)$ stops at zero but its image is a straight line, so a singular parameter need not mean singular geometry. The cusp $(t^{2},t^{3})$ has zero velocity at zero and requires a separate local analysis.

sections.title: Length and reparametrization
sections.text: For a piecewise continuously differentiable curve, length is $\int |r'(t)|dt$ over its pieces. A regular change of parameter preserves length after the speed factor and bounds are transformed. Unit tangent $r\prime/|r\prime|$ is defined only where speed is nonzero.

exercise.prompt: For $r(t)=(t,t^2)$, find speed and unit tangent at $t=1$.
exercise.hint: Differentiate components before taking the norm.
exercise.solution: $r'(1)=(1,2)$, speed $\sqrt{5}$, and unit tangent $(1,2)/\sqrt{5}$. The tangent line is $(1,1)+s(1,2)$.
rubric: Keep the selected point distinct from its velocity.
Normalize by speed.

sections.title: Graph, level set, parametrization
sections.text: A graph $z=f(x,y)$ has one height for each allowed planar input. A level set $F(x,y,z)=c$ may fail to be a graph in a chosen direction. A sphere has two $z$ values over most of its disk projection and needs upper and lower branches or surface charts.

sections.title: Read slices deliberately
sections.text: For $z=x^{2}-y^{2}$, fixing $y$ gives upward parabolas and fixing $x$ gives downward parabolas. Level zero is the pair $y=\pm x$; positive and negative levels give differently oriented hyperbolas. Distinguish a horizontal contour from a vertical slice.

exercise.prompt: Why is $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ not globally a graph $z=f(x,y)$?
exercise.hint: Inspect the two points above $(0,0)$.
exercise.solution: Both $(0,0,1)$ and $(0,0,-1)$ lie on the sphere. A single-valued graph cannot assign both heights; separate hemisphere graphs are possible over appropriate domains.
rubric: Use an explicit repeated planar input.
Distinguish local representation from global representation.
exercise.solutionTex: (0,0,1),(0,0,-1)\in S\implies S\text{ is not a single }z\text{-graph}

sections.title: Open balls encode all directions
sections.text: A ball $B(a,r)$ consists of points with distance less than $r$; its boundary sphere is excluded. A set is open when each member has some ball contained in it, and closed when it contains its limit points. A set can be neither open nor closed.

sections.title: Boundary depends on ambient space
sections.text: The disk $x^{2}+y^{2}<1$ is open in the plane, but the same disk embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ has no three-dimensional interior. For limits on a restricted domain, only points belonging to that domain are admissible approaches.

exercise.prompt: Classify the annulus $1<\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le 2$ as open, closed, or neither in $\mathbb R^2$.
exercise.hint: Test the included outer boundary and excluded inner boundary.
exercise.solution: It is neither: at an outer-circle point every ball leaves the set, while a sequence approaching the inner circle has a limit outside the set.
rubric: Name a witness against openness.
Name a missing limit point against closedness.

sections.title: One radius must cover every approach
sections.text: For a multivariable limit, every domain point with $0<|x-a|<\delta$ must meet the output tolerance. A separate $\delta$ for each ray is insufficient unless one common positive radius works uniformly.

sections.title: Use norm inequalities
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=2x-3y$ at zero, $|2x-3y|\leq \sqrt{13}\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Choosing $\delta =\varepsilon /\sqrt{13}$ proves the limit zero over every approach, including curved paths.

exercise.prompt: Prove $x^2+y^2$ tends to zero at the origin with an explicit $\delta$.
exercise.hint: Write the function in terms of the Euclidean radius $r$.
exercise.solution: The output is $r^{2}$. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose $\delta =\sqrt{\varepsilon }$; then $0<r<\delta$ gives $|f|<\varepsilon$.
rubric: Quantify over all domain points.
Use a radius independent of direction.

sections.title: Two paths can disprove
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=xy/(x^{2}+y^{2})$, the $x$-axis gives zero, while $y=x$ gives $1/2$ away from the origin. If a common limit existed, both admissible path restrictions would share it. Their difference proves nonexistence.

sections.title: Agreement cannot prove
sections.text: A finite or even infinite collection of selected paths can miss another obstruction. After path tests suggest a candidate, look for an estimate involving the full norm. The puncture and domain restrictions must hold along every path used.

exercise.prompt: For $x^2/(x^2+y^2)$, compare the two coordinate-axis limits at zero.
exercise.hint: Set $y=0$ and then $x=0$, excluding the origin.
exercise.solution: The $x$-axis gives 1 and the $y$-axis gives 0, so no limit exists.
rubric: Use two admissible paths approaching the same point.
State why distinct path limits contradict a common limit.

sections.title: Every line can agree
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=x^{2}y/(x^{4}+y^{2})$, along $y=mx$ with $m\ne 0$ the expression is $mx/(x^{2}+m^{2})\to 0$; along $y=0$ it is zero, and the vertical axis is zero. Thus every line through the origin suggests zero.

sections.title: A curve reveals the obstruction
sections.text: Along $y=x^{2}$ the same expression is $1/2$ for $x\ne 0$. The limit therefore fails. The denominator hints at the path: balance $x^{4}$ with $y^{2}$ by choosing $y$ proportional to $x^{2}$. Polar coordinates do not justify a limit unless the angular estimate is uniform.

exercise.prompt: What values occur along $y=kx^2$ for this function?
exercise.hint: Substitute and cancel $x^{4}$ for $x\ne 0$.
exercise.solution: The value is $k/(1+k^{2})$, independent of nonzero $x$. Different $k$ give different path limits and exhibit the hidden family of obstructions.
rubric: Balance denominator terms.
Cancel only away from the puncture.

sections.title: Squeeze with the full radius
sections.text: For $x^{2}y/(x^{2}+y^{2})$, use $|y|\leq r$ and $x^{2}/(x^{2}+y^{2})\leq 1$ to obtain $|f|\leq r$. Defining the value zero at the origin makes it continuous. This uniform estimate handles all paths at once.

sections.title: Composition has a target condition
sections.text: If $g$ tends to $b$ and $f$ is continuous at $b$ through the relevant domain, then $f\circ g$ tends to $f(b)$. Check that $g$’s nearby values lie in $f$’s domain; continuity of a formal expression outside its domain is not a usable theorem.

exercise.prompt: Does $xy/\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, extended by zero, become continuous at zero?
exercise.solution: Its absolute value is at most $r/2$ and therefore tends to zero. The extension is continuous.
rubric: Bound the absolute error by a quantity tending to zero.
Match the extension value to the limit.

sections.title: Every escape route counts
sections.text: A limit at infinity means for each $\varepsilon >0$ some $R$ makes the output error smaller than $\varepsilon$ whenever the input norm exceeds $R$ within the domain. Either coordinate can diverge; one cannot test only $x=y\to \infty$.

sections.title: A uniform decay estimate
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=1/(1+x^{2}+y^{2})$, if $r>R$ then $f<1/(1+R^{2})$. Choosing $R>1/\sqrt{\varepsilon }$ suffices to prove limit zero. The function $x^{2}/(x^{2}+y^{2})$, by contrast, retains values 1 or 0 on the coordinate axes even arbitrarily far away.

exercise.prompt: Does $x/(1+x^2+y^2)$ tend to zero at infinity?
exercise.hint: Bound $|x|$ by $r$.
exercise.solution: For $r>0$, its absolute value is at most $r/(1+r^{2})\leq 1/r$. Taking $R>1/\varepsilon$ proves the limit zero.
rubric: Use the full norm.
Give a single $R$ for every escape route.

supplementalBlocks.title: Slice slopes give only a candidate map
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Restrict the piecewise function to each coordinate axis before taking a quotient.

steps.label: Horizontal slice
steps.text: $q(h,0)=h$ for nonzero $h$, so $q_x(0,0)=1$.

steps.label: Candidate
steps.text: If a total derivative exists, it must send $(h,k)$ to $h$. This conclusion names the only possible map; it has not established a uniform remainder estimate.

supplementalBlocks.verification: The next step tests $|q(h,k)-L(h,k)|/\sqrt{h^2+k^2}$ along all approaches.

exercises.outcome: Distinguish coordinate slice slopes from continuity and total differentiability.
exercises.prompt: Extend $u(x,y)=xy/(x^2+y^2)$ by $u(0,0)=0$. Find both partials at zero from the definition, then test continuity along $y=x$.
exercises.hint: Both axis restrictions vanish, but the diagonal denominator is $2x^2$.
exercises.solution: Both axis restrictions are zero, hence both partials at zero equal zero. Along $(t,t)$ for $t\ne0$, $u(t,t)=1/2$, which does not tend to $u(0,0)=0$. It is discontinuous and cannot be totally differentiable there.
rubric: Use the actual axis restrictions at the piecewise point.
Give an admissible diagonal path.
Do not infer continuity from two partials.

sections.title: Hold the other input fixed
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=x^2y+\sin y$, $f_{x}=2xy$ and $f_y=x^2+\cos y$. The constant-held-fixed operation defines a coordinate slice derivative; it does not describe arbitrary combined input changes by itself.

sections.title: At a special point use the definition
sections.text: For a function defined by one formula away from zero and another at zero, differentiate the actual one-variable slice through zero. An off-origin derivative expression need not extend correctly by substitution at the missing point.

exercise.prompt: Find both partial derivatives of $f(x,y)=xe^y$ at $(2,0)$.
exercise.hint: In the $x$ derivative $e^y$ is constant; in the $y$ derivative $x$ is constant.
exercise.solution: $f_{x}=e^y$ gives 1 and $f_{y}=xe^y$ gives 2. These are the slopes of different coordinate slices at the same point.
rubric: Name which variable stays fixed.
Evaluate after differentiating.

sections.title: Cross product and rank
sections.text: For $u$,$v$ in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, $u\times v$ is perpendicular to both and has magnitude equal to their parallelogram area. If the vectors are dependent the product is zero, so it supplies no normal direction. Swapping the order reverses the normal.

sections.title: Write a plane from its normal
sections.text: For point $p$ and nonzero normal $n$, the plane is $n\cdot (x-p)=0$. With $u=(1,0,1)$, $v=(0,1,1)$, $u\times v=(-1,-1,1)$. Through $p=(0,0,2)$, the plane is $z=x+y+2$.

exercise.prompt: Find a normal and plane through the origin spanned by $(1,1,0)$ and $(0,1,1)$.
exercise.hint: Compute the ordered cross product.
exercise.solution: A normal is $(1,-1,1)$, giving $x-y+z=0$. Its dot product with each spanning vector is zero.
rubric: Check both orthogonality conditions.
Avoid confusing plane coefficients with a point on the plane.

supplementalBlocks.title: A derivative forces the slice slopes
supplementalBlocks.statement: If $f$ is totally differentiable at an interior point $a$, each coordinate partial exists and the derivative map is $Df(a)h=\sum_i f_{x_i}(a)h_i$.
hypotheses: $a$ is an interior point of the domain.

supplementalBlocks.title: Restrict the approximation to basis directions
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Set the full increment to a coordinate direction and read off each coefficient of the linear map.

steps.label: First coordinate
steps.text: Use $h=te_1$ and divide by nonzero $t$; $r(te_1)/t\to0$ because $|r(te_1)|/|t|\to0$.

steps.label: Other coordinates
steps.text: Repeat with every basis vector $e_i$; each partial equals $L(e_i)$.

steps.label: Linearity
steps.text: A linear map is determined by its basis values, so $Lh=\sum_i f_{x_i}(a)h_i$.

supplementalBlocks.result: The partials force a unique candidate; they do not prove its residual is small.
supplementalBlocks.verification: This is a one-way implication. The next lesson supplies a continuous function with all direction slopes but no total derivative.

supplementalBlocks.title: The full-radius remainder test
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Expand at an arbitrary base point and divide the residual by the full input distance.

steps.label: Expand
steps.text: The linear part is $2a_1h+2a_2k$ and the residual is $h^2+k^2$.

steps.label: Normalize
steps.text: For $r=\sqrt{h^2+k^2}>0$, the residual divided by $r$ equals $r$, independently of direction.

supplementalBlocks.verification: The bound covers every nonzero increment in the disk $r<\delta$, not selected lines alone.

exercises.outcome: Prove a candidate derivative with a full-radius bound.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^3$ at the origin, find the only candidate linear map and prove or disprove total differentiability using $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$.
exercises.hint: Both partials vanish. Bound $|x^2+y^3|/r$ with $|x|,|y|\le r$.
exercises.solution: The coordinate partials at zero are both zero, so $L=0$. For $0<r<1$, $|f|/r\le x^2/r+|y|^3/r\le r+r^2\to0$. Thus $f$ is totally differentiable at zero.
rubric: Identify the unique candidate map.
Use one norm bound valid for every direction.
Conclude from the normalized residual, not a plot.

sections.title: One linear map for all increments
sections.text: At a, differentiability means $f(a+h)=f(a)+Lh+r(h)$ with $r(h)/|h|\to 0$. For scalar $f$ with existing partials, the only candidate is $Lh=\nabla f(a)\cdot h$. The candidate still needs an all-direction remainder check.

sections.title: Work a polynomial remainder
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=x^{2}+y^{2}$ at $(a,b)$, the exact increment is $2ah+2bk+h^{2}+k^{2}$. Dividing the remainder by $\sqrt{h^{2}+k^{2}}$ gives $\sqrt{h^{2}+k^{2}}\to 0$, proving differentiability. The affine tangent plane includes the base value $a^{2}+b^{2}$.

exercise.prompt: Find and justify the derivative of $f(x,y)=xy$ at $(a,b)$.
exercise.hint: Expand $(a+h)(b+k)$ and bound |hk|.
exercise.solution: The linear map is $L(h,k)=bh+ak$. The remainder is hk, with $|hk|/\sqrt{h^{2}+k^{2}}\leq \sqrt{h^{2}+k^{2}}/2\to 0$.
rubric: Identify a linear map, not just two numbers.
Prove a uniform remainder bound.

supplementalBlocks.title: One continuous function defeats its candidate plane
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Use axis slices to find the candidate, then one diagonal to disprove its full-radius remainder condition.
supplementalBlocks.setup: $q(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ off zero, extended by $q(0,0)=0$; this is distinct from the final-review numerator $x^3-xy^2$.

steps.label: Continuity
steps.text: $|q(x,y)|\le|x|\le r$, so $q\to0$ as $r\to0$.

steps.label: Candidate
steps.text: The axis slices give $q_x(0)=1$, $q_y(0)=0$, forcing $L(x,y)=x$.

steps.label: Diagonal obstruction
steps.text: At $(t,t)$, $q=t/2$ and $L=t$; normalize their difference by $\sqrt2|t|$.

supplementalBlocks.result: $q$ is continuous with all directional derivatives, yet not totally differentiable at zero.
supplementalBlocks.verification: For $v=(a,b)\ne0$, $D_vq(0)=a^3/(a^2+b^2)$ is not additive in $v$; a total derivative would be linear.

exercises.outcome: Disprove total differentiability after computing the unique candidate and a normalized path residual.
exercises.prompt: Extend $p(x,y)=x^2y/(x^2+y^2)$ by zero at the origin. Find its coordinate partials and test total differentiability along $(t,t)$; also decide continuity.
exercises.hint: Both axis slices vanish. Along the diagonal, $p(t,t)=t/2$. Bound $|p|$ by a constant times $r$ for continuity.
exercises.solution: Both partials are zero, so $L=0$. For $t>0$, $|p(t,t)|/\sqrt{2t^{2}}=1/(2\sqrt{2})$, so no total derivative exists. Since $|p|=|y|x^{2}/r^{2}\leq |y|\leq r$, $p$ is continuous at zero.
rubric: Use definitions on the axes.
Normalize the diagonal remainder by Euclidean distance.
Prove continuity with an all-direction bound.

sections.title: Directional existence is weaker
sections.text: For the displayed $f(x,y)=x^{3}/(x^{2}+y^{2})$, extended by zero, every directional derivative along $v=(a,b)$ exists and equals $a^{3}/(a^{2}+b^{2})$. This dependence on $v$ is not linear, so it cannot be a total derivative. The final-review lesson studies the distinct numerator $x^{3}-xy^{2}$.

sections.title: Test the only possible map
sections.text: Coordinate partials give $L(x,y)=x$. Along $(t,t)$, $f=t/2$ while $L=t$, so $|f-L|/\sqrt{2t^{2}}=1/(2\sqrt{2})$. The normalized error does not vanish. Yet $|f|\leq r$, so $f$ is continuous: continuity is another distinct property.

exercise.prompt: For the displayed $f$, compare directional derivatives in $e_1$, $e_2$ and $e_1+e_2$.
exercise.hint: A linear derivative must preserve addition.
exercise.solution: They are 1, 0 and $1/2$ respectively. Since $1/2\ne 1+0$, the directional-derivative map is not additive, ruling out total differentiability.
rubric: Use directional vectors consistently without silently normalizing.
Test linearity explicitly.

supplementalBlocks.title: Continuous partials are sufficient (imported)
supplementalBlocks.statement: If every first partial derivative exists near $a$ and is continuous at $a$, then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$.
hypotheses: All first partials exist on a neighborhood of $a$ and are continuous at $a$.
prerequisites: Mean value theorem applied to coordinate increments

supplementalBlocks.title: Choose the proof route
supplementalBlocks.text: The $C^1$ criterion is sufficient, not necessary. If its neighborhood hypotheses fail, it gives no verdict; compute the unique candidate from partials and test the normalized residual directly. The exact final-review pair lets you compare a successful all-direction bound with a failed diagonal bound.

exercises.outcome: Distinguish a sufficient $C^1$ criterion from the definition of differentiability.
exercises.prompt: Let $f(x,y)=|xy|$. At the origin, show differentiability directly. Can you apply the theorem requiring first partials throughout a neighborhood?
exercises.hint: Use $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$. At nearby points on an axis, check the partial in the transverse direction.
exercises.solution: Both coordinate partials at zero are zero, so $L=0$. Since $|f|/r\leq r/2\to 0$, $f$ is differentiable at zero. At $(0,y)$ with $y\ne 0$, the $x$ partial of |xy| does not exist, so the continuous-partials neighborhood theorem is unavailable. Its failure does not reverse the conclusion.
rubric: Prove differentiability with a uniform norm bound.
Identify a failed neighborhood hypothesis.
Do not treat a sufficient theorem as necessary.

sections.title: A useful sufficient theorem
sections.text: If all first partial derivatives exist on a neighborhood and are continuous at a, then $f$ is differentiable at a. This $C^1$ criterion is sufficient, not necessary. Partial derivatives existing only at a do not satisfy it.

sections.title: Finite versus asymptotic error
sections.text: If a twice continuously differentiable $f$ has Hessian operator norm at most $M$ along the segment from a to $a+h$, Taylor gives $|f(a+h)-f(a)-\nabla f(a)\cdot h|\leq M|h|^{2}/2$. This finite bound needs an actual $M$; little-o alone does not provide one.

exercise.prompt: Bound the tangent-plane error for $f=x^2+y^2$ at any base point when $|h|\le 0.01$.
exercise.hint: The Hessian is twice the identity.
exercise.solution: $M=2$, so the error is at most $|h|^{2}\leq 0.0001$. Here the remainder equals $|h|^{2}$ exactly.
rubric: Control the Hessian along the whole segment.
Distinguish a guaranteed bound from a sampled error.

supplementalBlocks.title: Composition multiplies the linear parts
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Apply one differentiability expansion to the path and another to the field.

steps.label: Path increment
steps.text: $k=r(t+h)-r(t)$ is $O(|h|)$ because the path is differentiable.

steps.label: Field increment
steps.text: Substitute that $k$ into the field expansion. Since $\|k\|=O(|h|)$, the field remainder is $o(|h|)$.
steps.usesHypothesis: $f$ totally differentiable at $r(t)$; coordinate partials alone are insufficient.

steps.label: Linear coefficient
steps.text: The remaining first-order term is $Df(r(t))r'(t)h$.

supplementalBlocks.verification: For $f=x^2+y^2$ and $r(t)=(t,t^2)$, both direct differentiation and the dot product give $2t+4t^3$.

exercises.outcome: Compute a composed rate with both coordinate contributions and verify it directly.
exercises.prompt: For $f(x,y)=xy$ and $r(t)=(t^2,t^3)$, compute $(f\circ r)'(t)$ by the multivariable chain rule and by first composing. Name the differentiability assumptions.
exercises.hint: Use $\nabla f=(y,x)$ and $r'=(2t,3t^2)$.
exercises.solution: The dot product is $(t^{3},t^{2})\cdot (2t,3t^{2})=5t^{4}$. Directly, $f(r(t))=t^{5}$ also differentiates to $5t^{4}$. Both $f$ and $r$ are polynomial maps, hence differentiable everywhere.
rubric: Evaluate the field derivative along the path.
Include both coordinate rates.
Check the composed expression and assumptions.

sections.title: Do not hide cancellation
sections.text: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ and $r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$, the output is constant and its derivative zero. To see nonzero contributions, take $r(t)=(t,t^2)$: $f(r(t))=t^2+t^4$ and derivative $2t+4t^3$.

sections.title: Multiply derivative maps
sections.text: Along that path, $\nabla f(r(t))=(2t,2t^{2})$ and $r'(t)=(1,2t)$, whose dot product is $2t+4t^{3}$. More generally $D(f\circ g)=Df(g)Dg$, with matrix dimensions determined by the input and output spaces. Differentiability of both maps is a sufficient hypothesis.

exercise.prompt: For $f(x,y)=xe^y$ and $r(t)=(t,t^2)$, find $d(f\circ r)/dt$.
exercise.hint: Compute the two partial contributions separately.
exercise.solution: The derivative is $e^{t^2}\cdot 1+t e^{t^2}\cdot 2t=e^{t^2}(1+2t^2)$, agreeing with direct differentiation of $t e^{t^2}$.
rubric: Evaluate partials on the path.
Include both coordinate rates.
Check using the composed formula.

sections.title: Which variable can be solved for?
sections.text: For a $C^1$ equation $F(x,y,z)=0$, if $F_z(p)\ne0$ then a local $C^1$ graph $z=g(x,y)$ exists near $p$. Its derivatives are $g_x=-F_x/F_z$ and $g_y=-F_y/F_z$. This existence theorem is imported; differentiating a presumed graph alone does not prove its existence.

sections.title: Choose another chart when needed
sections.text: On the unit sphere at $(0,0,1)$, $F_z=2$ and a local $z$ graph exists. At $(1,0,0)$, $F_z=0$ but $F_x=2$, so $x$ can instead be expressed locally as a function of $y,z$. The surface remains smooth even though a chosen graph direction fails.

exercise.prompt: Find the tangent plane to $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$ at $(1,2,2)$.
exercise.hint: Use the nonzero gradient as normal.
rubric: Verify the point is on the surface.
Use a nonzero gradient.

supplementalBlocks.title: The gradient formula needs one linear map
supplementalBlocks.statement: If $f$ is totally differentiable at $p$, then $D_uf(p)=Df(p)u=\nabla f(p)\cdot u$ for any fixed vector $u$.
hypotheses: $p$ is an interior point and $f$ is totally differentiable there.
$u$ is fixed; choose $\|u\|=1$ for rate per unit distance.

supplementalBlocks.title: Restrict the full error to one line
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Substitute $h=tu$ in the full differentiability expansion.

steps.label: Restriction
steps.text: $f(p+tu)-f(p)=tDf(p)u+r(tu)$ by linearity.

steps.label: Divide
steps.text: $r(tu)/t$ tends to zero because $|r(tu)|/|t|=\|u\| |r(tu)|/\|tu\|\to0$.
steps.usesHypothesis: The remainder condition holds for all small vectors, hence this line.

supplementalBlocks.result: $D_uf(p)=Df(p)u$. Unit normalization changes interpretation, not existence.
supplementalBlocks.verification: The reverse implication is false; the preceding counterexample has every directional derivative but no total derivative.

exercises.outcome: Check total differentiability before replacing a directional limit by a gradient dot product.
exercises.prompt: For $q(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ off zero and $q(0)=0$, compare $D_{(1,1)}q(0)$ from its defining limit with $\nabla q(0)\cdot(1,1)$. Why may they differ?
exercises.hint: Along $(t,t)$, $q(t,t)=t/2$; axis partials are $(1,0)$.
exercises.solution: The defining limit gives $D_(1,1)q(0)=1/2$. The axis partials form gradient $(1,0)$, whose dot product with $(1,1)$ is 1. The dot-product theorem requires total differentiability, which fails for this $q$.
rubric: Use the unnormalized vector consistently.
Compute the directional limit directly.
Name the missing total-differentiability hypothesis.

sections.title: Normalize when measuring slope per distance
sections.text: For a differentiable scalar field, $D_{u}f=\nabla f\cdot u$. A unit $u$ measures change per unit distance; an arbitrary velocity $v$ includes its speed. For $f=x^{2}+3y^{2}$ at $(1,1)$, the gradient is $(2,6)$, so direction $(1,1)/\sqrt{2}$ gives slope $4\sqrt{2}$.

sections.title: Existence of the gradient is not the whole hypothesis
sections.text: Coordinate partials define a vector when they exist, but the dot-product formula for all directions is guaranteed by total differentiability. At singular examples, compute the directional derivative from its limit rather than assuming the formula.

exercise.prompt: Find the directional derivative of $f=x^2+y^2$ at $(1,2)$ in direction $(3,4)$.
exercise.hint: Normalize $(3,4)$ to length one.
exercise.solution: The gradient is $(2,4)$, so the unit-direction derivative is $(2,4)\cdot (3/5,4/5)=22/5$. Using velocity $(3,4)$ instead would give 22 per unit time.
rubric: Declare whether the vector is a direction or a velocity.
Evaluate the gradient at the requested point.

supplementalBlocks.title: Maximal first-order slope
supplementalBlocks.statement: At a totally differentiable point, the largest directional derivative over unit $u$ is $\|\nabla f(p)\|$.
hypotheses: $u$ has unit length; if $\nabla f(p)\ne0$, normalize the gradient to identify a maximizing direction.

supplementalBlocks.title: Bound every unit direction
supplementalBlocks.strategy: Optimize the linear first-order response using Cauchy–Schwarz.

steps.label: Upper bound
steps.text: Cauchy–Schwarz gives $D_uf(p)\le|D_uf(p)|\le\|\nabla f(p)\|$.
steps.usesHypothesis: Total differentiability supplies the dot product formula.

steps.label: Equality
steps.text: If the gradient is nonzero, choose $u=\nabla f/\|\nabla f\|$; its dot product equals the norm.

steps.label: Stationary case
steps.text: If the gradient vanishes, all first-order directional slopes are zero, with no distinguished maximizing direction.

supplementalBlocks.result: The maximal first-order slope is $\|\nabla f(p)\|$.
supplementalBlocks.verification: This local linear statement does not promise globally increasing values along a finite step.

exercises.outcome: Interpret a zero gradient without inventing a unique ascent direction.
exercises.prompt: At the origin for $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$, what is the maximum unit directional derivative and which unit directions attain it? Does that say nearby values cannot increase?
exercises.hint: Compute the gradient at zero, then compare actual function values at nonzero nearby points.
exercises.solution: The gradient is zero, so every unit direction has first-order directional derivative zero; the maximum is zero and every unit direction attains it. Yet $f(x,y)=x^{2}+y^{2}>0$ at every nonzero nearby point, a second-order increase.
rubric: State the maximum slope and all maximizing unit directions.
Separate first-order slope from finite nearby values.
Do not claim a unique direction at zero gradient.

sections.title: The maximum slope is a norm
sections.text:
Cauchy–Schwarz gives $
abla f\cdot u\leq |
abla f|$ for unit $u$, with equality for $u=
abla f/|
abla f|$ when $
abla f
e 0$. At a stationary point all first-order slopes vanish, so the gradient picks no unique steepest direction.

sections.title: Contours and tangency
sections.text: If a differentiable curve lies in $f=c$, chain rule gives $\nabla f\cdot r'=0$. A nonzero gradient is normal to the level set. A zero gradient does not establish a smooth contour or a normal direction; inspect the geometry separately.

exercise.prompt: At $(1,1)$, find the steepest ascent direction for $f=x^2+2y^2$ and the maximum slope.
exercise.hint: Use gradient $(2,4)$.
exercise.solution: Its norm is $2\sqrt{5}$, and the unit direction is $(1,2)/\sqrt{5}$. The opposite direction gives steepest descent.
rubric: Normalize the direction.
Distinguish maximum slope from the direction vector.

sections.title: Use the domain in the definition
sections.text: A local minimum compares values in some neighborhood intersected with the domain. Interior differentiable extrema require zero gradient; boundary extrema do not. A saddle has nearby values on both sides of the point’s value.

sections.title: Stationarity admits every outcome
sections.text: At the origin, $x^{2}+y^{2}$ has a strict minimum, $-x^{2}-y^{2}$ a strict maximum, and $x^{2}-y^{2}$ a saddle. The zero function has non-strict maxima and minima everywhere. All have zero gradient at the origin.

exercise.prompt: Classify $f(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ at zero directly.
exercise.hint: Compare its coordinate axes.
exercise.solution: Along $(t,0)$, $f=t^{2}>0$; along $(0,t)$, $f=-t^{2}<0$ for nonzero $t$. Arbitrarily close values lie above and below $f(0,0)=0$, so the point is a saddle.
rubric: Produce both signs arbitrarily close.
Do not identify a saddle from stationarity alone.

sections.title: Order and notation
sections.text: Here $f_{xy}$ means differentiate first in $x$ and then in $y$. For $f=x^{2}y^{3}$, $f_{xy}=6xy^{2}=f_{yx}$. State the convention because subscript and operator notation are sometimes read in different orders.

sections.title: When swapping is justified
sections.text: Continuity of the second partials on a neighborhood is a sufficient condition for equality of mixed partials. Merely existing at one point is insufficient. Higher-order cancellation identities likewise need appropriate smoothness rather than formal rearrangement alone.

exercise.prompt: Compute both mixed partials of $f=xe^y+y \sin x$.
exercise.hint: Differentiate in the stated order each time.
exercise.solution: $f_x=e^y+y\cos x$, so $f_{xy}=e^y+\cos x$. Also $f_y=xe^y+\sin x$, so $f_{yx}=e^y+\cos x$. Smoothness justifies equality.
rubric: Show both orders.
Name a sufficient regularity condition.

sections.title: Quadratic forms decide second-order shape
sections.text: For a $C^{2}$ scalar field at a stationary point, the quadratic Taylor term is $h^{T}Hh/2$. A positive-definite Hessian gives a strict minimum, a negative-definite one a strict maximum, and an indefinite one a saddle. In two dimensions, determinant positive plus $f_{xx}>0$ or $f_{xx}<0$ distinguishes the two definite cases.

sections.title: Mixed terms can rotate the shape
sections.text: For $f=x^{2}+4xy+y^{2}$, $H=[[2,4],[4,2]]$ has eigenvalues 6 and $-2$. Coordinate-axis slices both rise, yet along $y=-x$ the value is $-2x^{2}$, so it is a saddle. A zero determinant is inconclusive; compare $x^{4}+y^{4}$ with $x^{4}-y^{4}$.

exercise.prompt: Classify $f=-2x^2-2xy-2y^2$ at zero.
exercise.hint: Compute the Hessian determinant and one diagonal entry.
exercise.solution: $H=[[-4,-2],[-2,-4]]$, determinant $12>0$ and $f_{xx}<0$, so it is negative definite and zero is a strict local maximum. Completing squares also shows global maximality.
rubric: Retain the mixed-term contribution.
State local classification and justify any global claim separately.

sections.title: Existence then candidate search
sections.text: A continuous function on a nonempty compact set attains maximum and minimum. Search interior stationary points, smooth boundary stationary points, corners, and singular locations. A local Hessian test does not compare all candidates.

sections.title: A disk example
sections.text: For $f=x^{2}+y^{2}-2x$ on the closed unit disk, the unconstrained stationary point is $(1,0)$, on the boundary. On the boundary $f=1-2x$, so its values range from $-1$ at $(1,0)$ to 3 at $(-1,0)$. Completing the square $f=(x-1)^{2}+y^{2}-1$ confirms the minimum.

exercise.prompt: Find extrema of $f=x+y$ on the square $[0,1]^2$.
exercise.hint: There are no interior stationary points; inspect the boundary and corners.
exercise.solution: The minimum is 0 at $(0,0)$, maximum 2 at $(1,1)$. Monotonicity in each coordinate proves these global bounds.
rubric: Include boundary candidates.
Explain attainment on the closed bounded set.

sections.title: Tangency is a necessary condition
sections.text:
For a smooth constraint $g=c$ with $
abla g
e 0$, a constrained extremum has $
abla f=\lambda 
abla g$. Both gradients are normal to the same tangent directions. Solve the multiplier equations together with the original constraint.

sections.title: A singular constraint can hide candidates
sections.text: For $g(x,y)=x^{3}-y^{2}=0$ at zero, $\nabla g=0$. The usual regular multiplier condition cannot be assumed there. Keep such feasible singular points as separate candidates instead of dividing by a gradient component.

exercise.prompt: Find the extrema of $x+y$ on $x^2+y^2=1$.
exercise.hint: The equations $1=2\lambda x$ and $1=2\lambda y$ force $x=y$.
exercise.solution: The candidates are $(\pm 1/\sqrt{2},\pm 1/\sqrt{2})$ with matching signs, giving $\pm \sqrt{2}$. Compactness ensures extrema, and Cauchy–Schwarz independently bounds $|x+y|\leq \sqrt{2}$.
rubric: Keep the constraint equation.
Compare all candidates and justify globality.

sections.title: One constraint leaves a tangent plane
sections.text:
On a regular level surface in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, tangent vectors are perpendicular to $
abla g$. At a constrained extremum the derivative of $f$ vanishes along that entire plane, making $
abla f$ a multiple of $
abla g$.

sections.title: Linear objective on a sphere
sections.text: For $f=x+2y+2z$ on the unit sphere, $\nabla f=(1,2,2)$ and $\nabla g=2(x,y,z)$. The candidates are $\pm (1,2,2)/3$, giving values $\pm 3$. Norm comparison proves these are global extrema.

exercise.prompt: Maximize $2x-y+2z$ on $x^2+y^2+z^2=4$.
exercise.hint: Use Cauchy–Schwarz or solve the multiplier equations.
exercise.solution: The coefficient vector has norm 3 and the sphere radius is 2, so the maximum is 6 at $(4/3,-2/3,4/3)$.
rubric: Scale the maximizing unit vector by the radius.
Check the point satisfies the constraint.

sections.title: Independence matters
sections.text:
For two constraints $g=c$ and $h=d$ in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, independent gradients give a tangent direction $
abla g	imes 
abla h$. At a constrained extremum, $
abla f$ lies in their span: $
abla f=\lambda 
abla g+\mu 
abla h$. Dependent gradients invalidate this regular argument.

sections.title: Reduce when possible
sections.text: On $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=1$ and $z=0$, maximizing $x+y$ reduces to the unit circle in the xy-plane. The two gradients $(2x,2y,0)$ and $(0,0,1)$ are independent everywhere on the feasible circle, so the multiplier method is legitimate.

exercise.prompt: Find extrema of $x$ on $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ with $y=z$.
exercise.hint: Either use two multipliers or observe the feasible circle contains $(\pm 1,0,0)$.
exercise.solution: Since $|x|\leq 1$ on the sphere and both $(\pm 1,0,0)$ satisfy $y=z$, extrema are $\pm 1$ at those points. The constraint gradients are independent throughout the intersection.
rubric: Check feasibility of equality cases.
Identify the regularity assumption when using multipliers.

sections.title: Cells contribute value times area
sections.text: Over a rectangle, a double Riemann sum adds $f(\text{sample})\Delta x\Delta y$. Both widths are essential. Integrability requires independence of increasingly fine tagged partitions; a single sampled mesh is a numerical approximation.

sections.title: Signed volume versus physical volume
sections.text: If $f\geq 0$, the integral is volume under its graph. If $f$ takes both signs, it is signed accumulation. For $f=x$ on $[-1,1]\times [0,1]$, the integral is zero while the volume between graph and plane is $\int |x|=1$.

exercise.prompt: Compute the double integral of constant 3 over $[0,2]\times [0,4]$.
exercise.hint: Every cell contributes three times its area.
exercise.solution: The rectangle area is 8, so the integral is 24. With density units $kg/m^{2}$ and coordinates in metres, the result is kilograms.
rubric: Include both dimensions of area.
Interpret the units of the integrand.

sections.title: A sufficient computational framework
sections.text: For a bounded region with a boundary of area zero and a function continuous on its closure, the double integral can be defined by extending the function by zero to a containing rectangle. The extension may jump at the region boundary but remains Riemann integrable under these sufficient assumptions.

sections.title: Name the stronger theorem
sections.text: The criterion that a bounded function on a rectangle is Riemann integrable when its discontinuity set has area zero is imported here. Lebesgue integration extends beyond Jordan regions and is an optional advanced framework, not a prerequisite silently hidden inside the elementary continuous-rectangle theorem.

exercise.prompt: Why can a continuous density on a disk be extended by zero for integration on a containing square?
exercise.hint: Where can new discontinuities occur?
exercise.solution: Only the circular boundary can acquire jumps. That boundary has area zero, so the bounded zero extension is Riemann integrable by the stated criterion. Its integral equals the disk integral.
rubric: Identify the possible discontinuity set.
Invoke the appropriate extension theorem.

sections.title: Order is a theorem, not typography
sections.text: A continuous function on a closed rectangle has equal double and iterated integrals. For zero extensions over ordinary piecewise smooth regions, a stronger integrability version is required because the extension may have boundary jumps.

sections.title: A sufficient extension for calculations
sections.text: For a bounded Riemann-integrable function whose slices are integrable apart from finitely many exceptional outer values, the iterated integrals agree with the double integral; changing bounded values on those exceptional slices does not affect it. In the Lebesgue setting, absolute integrability permits Fubini and nonnegativity permits Tonelli, but those are separate imported results.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\int_0^1\int_0^2(x+y)\,dy\,dx$ in both orders.
exercise.hint: The rectangle and continuous polynomial satisfy the elementary theorem.
exercise.solution: Integrating in $y$ gives $2x+2$, then total 3. Reversing gives $\int_0^2(1/2+y)\,dy=3$. The domain remains the same rectangle.
rubric: State why the swap is valid.
Keep each variable’s interval attached to it.

sections.title: Bounds describe a set
sections.text: The region $0\leq x\leq 1$, $x^{2}\leq y\leq x$ lies between a parabola and a line. For horizontal slices, $0\leq y\leq 1$ and $y\leq x\leq \sqrt{y}$. Derive these inequalities before changing the integration order.

sections.title: Split when one slice formula fails
sections.text: A region may need several Type I or Type II pieces. Splitting along an internal boundary does not duplicate area if pieces overlap only on boundaries of area zero. Draw or solve each boundary intersection and determine which curve actually limits a slice.

exercise.prompt: Reverse $\int_0^1\int_{x^2}^x f(x,y)\,dy\,dx$.
exercise.hint: Solve $y\geq x^{2}$ and $y\leq x$ in the nonnegative quadrant.
exercise.solution: The reversed integral is $\int_0^1\int_y^{\sqrt{y}}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy$. The conditions give $x\leq \sqrt{y}$ and $x\geq y$.
rubric: Derive both horizontal bounds.
Preserve the region and integrand.

sections.title: Linearity concerns values
sections.text: For integrable $f$,$g$, $\int (af+bg)=a\int f+b\int g$. It does not assert that $\int fg=(\int f)(\int g)$. A product separates only under additional structure, such as independent factors on a product rectangle.

sections.title: Additivity concerns regions
sections.text: If a region is split into pieces overlapping only on negligible boundaries, add their integrals. For signed accumulation, negative contributions remain negative. Overlapping pieces with positive area require subtracting the overlap to avoid double counting.

exercise.prompt: If $\iint_D f\,dA=2$ and $\iint_D g\,dA=-1$, find $\iint_D(3f-2g)\,dA$. Can you infer $\iint_D fg\,dA$?
exercise.hint: Apply linearity only to the linear combination.
exercise.solution: The first integral is $3\cdot 2-2\cdot (-1)=8$. The product integral cannot be determined from these two numbers alone.
rubric: Handle the negative coefficient.
Do not invent multiplicativity.

sections.title: Derive the factor geometrically
sections.text: A polar cell has radial thickness $dr$ and transverse length approximately $r\,d\theta$, so area is approximately $r\,dr\,d\theta$. The derivative columns of $(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ have determinant $r$, confirming the local scale for $r\ge0$.

sections.title: A coordinate singularity is not a hole
sections.text: At $r=0$ all angles describe one point and the determinant vanishes. For standard disk integrals this point has area zero and can be handled by a limiting argument. Angular endpoints also represent the same ray when using a full $2\pi$ interval.

exercise.prompt: Compute the area of the annular sector $1\le r\le 2$, $0\le \theta\le \pi/3$.
exercise.hint: Integrate the Jacobian $r$, not 1.
exercise.solution: The area is $\int_0^{\pi/3}\int_1^2r\,dr\,d\theta=(\pi /3)(3/2)=\pi /2$.
rubric: Include the radial factor.
Distinguish parameter-rectangle area from physical area.

sections.title: Derive the shifted disk
sections.text: For $(x-1)^2+y^2\le1$, substitute polar coordinates to get $r^2-2r\cos\theta\le0$. With $r\ge0$ and $r>0$ this gives $0<r\le2\cos\theta$, so $\cos\theta\ge0$. Choose $-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2$, with $r=0$ included separately.

sections.title: Verify the area
sections.text: The integral is $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\int_0^{2\cos\theta}r\,dr\,d\theta=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}2\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\pi$. This matches a disk of radius one. A centered fixed-radius sector would represent a different region.

exercise.prompt: Write polar bounds for $(x-2)^2+y^2\le 4$.
exercise.hint: Repeat the algebra with center and radius 2.
exercise.solution: The bounds are $-\pi /2\leq \theta \leq \pi /2$ and $0\leq r\leq 4cos \theta$. The area is $4\pi$, matching the disk radius 2.
rubric: Derive the angular range from nonnegative radius.
Handle the origin without dividing by zero.

sections.title: Volume cells need three widths
sections.text: A triple sum adds $f(\text{sample})\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z$. For $f=1$ it approximates volume; for mass density it approximates mass. A display containing only a few columns is a schematic, not a complete three-dimensional partition.

sections.title: Check a separable box
sections.text: For $f=xyz$ on $[0,1]\times [0,2]\times [0,3]$, continuity allows repeated integration and the product structure separates the result into $(1/2)\cdot 2\cdot (9/2)=9$. This separation depends on both the factorized integrand and rectangular domain.

exercise.prompt: Integrate constant density 5 on a box with side lengths 2,3,4.
exercise.hint: Multiply density by the volume.
exercise.solution: The integral is $5\cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot 4=120$. If density is $kg/m^{3}$, this is mass in kg.
rubric: Include all three dimensions.
Interpret the measure and units.

sections.title: Project before setting height bounds
sections.text: The tetrahedron $x,y,z\geq 0$ with $x+y+z\leq 1$ projects onto $x,y\geq 0$, $x+y\leq 1$. Thus $0\leq x\leq 1$, $0\leq y\leq 1-x$, $0\leq z\leq 1-x-y$. The inner bounds depend only on outer variables.

sections.title: Each order describes the same solid
sections.text: A different outer coordinate requires a different projection. Writing all upper limits as 1 would replace the tetrahedron by a cube. Integrating 1 over the correct bounds gives volume $1/6$.

exercise.prompt: Write bounds with $x$ innermost for the same tetrahedron.
exercise.hint: Project onto the yz-plane.
exercise.solution: Use $0\leq z\leq 1$, $0\leq y\leq 1-z$, $0\leq x\leq 1-y-z$. Integrating 1 again yields $1/6$.
rubric: Derive the outer projection.
Keep an inner bound free of its own integration variable.

sections.title: A planar polar map plus height
sections.text: Cylindrical coordinates are $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$, $z=z$ with $r\ge0$. The volume Jacobian is $r$. The angle is measured around the $z$-axis; it does not tilt toward that axis.

sections.title: Identify surfaces by equations
sections.text: $r=2$ is a cylinder, $z=2$ a horizontal plane, and $z=r$ a cone above the plane. The $z$-axis has $r=0$ and nonunique $\theta$; this coordinate singularity does not remove the axis from a solid.

exercise.prompt: Convert $x^2+y^2\le 4$ and $1\le z\le 3$ into cylindrical bounds.
exercise.hint: The planar projection is a full disk.
exercise.solution: $0\leq r\leq 2$, $0\leq \theta \leq 2\pi$, $1\leq z\leq 3$, with volume element $r$ dr $d\theta$ dz in a compatible chosen order.
rubric: Include the full angular range.
Use the factor $r$ for volume.

sections.title: Transform bounds and integrand
sections.text: Between $z=r^{2}$ and $z=4$, the surfaces meet at $r=2$. Volume is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\int_{r^2}^4 r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=8\pi$. An integrand $x^{2}+y^{2}$ becomes $r^{2}$, creating $r^{3}$ after multiplication by the Jacobian.

sections.title: Do not count the Jacobian twice
sections.text: The measure $r$ dr $d\theta$ dz already accounts for geometric stretching. If the physical density is itself $r$, the total factor $r^{2}$ has two different origins: density and volume measure. Label them separately.

exercise.prompt: Find the integral of $x^2+y^2$ over the cylinder of radius 1 and height 2.
exercise.hint: Use density $r^{2}$ and measure $r$.
exercise.solution: The result is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1\int_0^2r^3\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=\pi$.
rubric: Transform the scalar field.
Multiply by one volume Jacobian.

sections.title: Fix the angle convention
sections.text: Use $\rho\ge0$, azimuth $\theta$ around the $z$-axis, and polar angle $\varphi$ down from the positive $z$-axis: $x=\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta$, $y=\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta$, $z=\rho\cos\varphi$. Standard ranges are $0\le\theta<2\pi$ and $0\le\varphi\le\pi$.

sections.title: Distinguish coordinate singularities
sections.text: At $\rho =0$ every angle pair represents the origin. At $\varphi =0$ or $\pi$ the azimuth is nonunique. These failures of coordinates do not imply the sphere or solid is geometrically singular.

exercise.prompt: What spherical coordinates describe $(0,0,-2)$?
exercise.hint: The point lies on the negative polar axis.
exercise.solution: $\rho =2$ and $\varphi =\pi$; any $\theta$ represents the same point. The nonunique azimuth is expected.
rubric: State the polar-angle convention.
Allow nonunique coordinates on the axis.

contentBlocks.title: A sphere centered away from the origin
contentBlocks.strategy: Convert each surface separately, then intersect the allowed angle and radial intervals before integrating.
contentBlocks.setup: Let $E$ lie above $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and inside $x^2+y^2+z^2=z$, as posed in MH2100 Lecture 07, physical page 50. Derive its bounds before evaluating the volume.

steps.label: Cone selects directions
steps.text: For $\rho\ge0$, the cone inequality becomes $\rho\cos\varphi\ge\rho\sin\varphi$. Except at the origin this gives $0\le\varphi\le\pi/4$; rotational symmetry gives $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.

steps.label: Sphere sets a variable radial ceiling
steps.text: The sphere inequality is $\rho^2\le\rho\cos\varphi$. The origin is included, and for positive radius the upper bound is $\cos\varphi$, not a constant.

steps.label: Integrate the actual solid
steps.text: Use density $1$ and exactly one spherical volume factor $\rho^2\sin\varphi$. Integrating first in radius gives $\cos^3\varphi/3$.

contentBlocks.result: The exact volume is $\pi/8$; replacing $\cos\varphi$ by a fixed sphere radius changes the region.
contentBlocks.verification: At $\varphi=0$ the radial ceiling is $1$; at $\varphi=\pi/4$ it is $1/\sqrt2$. The sphere is centered at $(0,0,1/2)$ with radius $1/2$, so a constant radial ceiling about the origin cannot describe it.

sections.title: Three scale factors
sections.text: A small spherical cell has lengths approximately $d\rho$, $\rho\,d\varphi$ and $\rho\sin\varphi\,d\theta$. Its volume factor is $\rho^2\sin\varphi$. The signed determinant depends on coordinate order; scalar volume uses its absolute value.

sections.title: Cone and sphere bounds
sections.text: Inside a sphere of radius $R$ and above the cone $\varphi =\pi /4$, use $0\leq \rho \leq R$, $0\leq \varphi \leq \pi /4$, $0\leq \theta \leq 2\pi$. Volume is $(2\pi R^{3}/3)(1-1/\sqrt{2})$, not a cylinder sector.

sections.title: Shifted spheres need variable radial bounds
sections.text: For a sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=cz$ with $c>0$, the interior is $0\leq\rho\leq c\cos\varphi$ where $\cos\varphi\ge0$. An intersecting cone $z\geq\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ restricts directions to $0\leq\varphi\leq\pi/4$. These inequalities specify the same physical solid before any Jacobian is applied.

exercise.prompt: Integrate $x^2+y^2+z^2$ over the ball of radius $R$.
exercise.hint: The integrand is $\rho^2$ and the measure adds another $\rho^2\sin\varphi$.
exercise.solution: The integral is $(R^{5}/5)\cdot 2\cdot 2\pi =4\pi R^{5}/5$. For $R=1$ it is $4\pi /5$.
rubric: Use the full polar range.
Separate the integrand from the Jacobian.

exercises.outcome: Derive a variable spherical radial bound and transform a nonconstant density independently of the Jacobian.
exercises.prompt: Let $D$ lie above $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and inside $x^2+y^2+z^2=2z$. Set spherical bounds and compute $\iiint_D z\,dV$.
exercises.hint: The cone still limits $\varphi$ to $[0,\pi/4]$. Divide the sphere inequality by positive $\rho$, then keep the density $z=\rho\cos\varphi$ separate from $dV$.
exercises.solution: The sphere gives $0\le\rho\le2\cos\varphi$, while $0\le\varphi\le\pi/4$ and $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. The density times the volume factor is $\rho^3\cos\varphi\sin\varphi$. Radial integration gives $4\cos^5\varphi\sin\varphi$, so the integral is $8\pi(1-(1/\sqrt2)^6)/6=7\pi/6$.
rubric: Derive the radial bound from the shifted sphere, not a constant-radius ball.
Use the cone for the polar angle and all azimuths.
Transform the density and include the volume factor once.

sections.title: Columns are transformed edges
sections.text: For $A=[[2,1],[0,3]]$, the unit square edges map to $(2,0)$ and $(1,3)$. Their parallelogram area is |det $A|=6$. Every cell has the same area scale because the map is linear.

sections.title: Orientation and collapse
sections.text: A negative determinant reverses orientation while keeping positive area scale. A zero determinant collapses the plane into a line or point, so a two-dimensional inverse does not exist. The determinant is a number; the derivative matrix is a different object.

exercise.prompt: Find signed and unsigned area factors for $T(u,v)=(u,-2v)$.
exercise.hint: Use the diagonal derivative matrix.
exercise.solution: The signed determinant is $-2$ and area scale is 2. The map reverses orientation.
rubric: Keep sign for orientation.
Use absolute value for scalar area.

sections.title: A nonlinear map with variable scale
sections.text: Let $T(u,v)=(u,(1+u)v)$, $0\leq u,v\leq 1$. Its derivative columns are $(1,v)$ and $(0,1+u)$, so det $DT=1+u$. The image is $0\leq x\leq 1$, $0\leq y\leq 1+x$: a trapezoid with area $3/2$.

sections.title: Finite cells versus infinitesimal cells
sections.text: For $T(u,v)=(u,(1+u)v)$, the exact image area of $[u,u+h]\times [v,v+k]$ is $hk(1+u+h/2)$. Its finite scale approaches $1+u$ as $h\to 0$. The separate shrinking-cell experiment uses $T(u,v)=(u,v+uv^{2})$. Its exact ratio is $1+2(u+h/2)(v+k/2)$, while det $DT=1+2uv$. With $k$ fixed and $h\to 0$, bias uk remains: the cell diameter does not vanish. Shrinking $h$ and $k$ together makes diameter $\sqrt{h^{2}+k^{2}}$ tend to zero and recovers the local determinant.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\iint_R y\,dA$ over that trapezoid using $T$.
exercise.hint: Replace $y$ by $(1+u)v$ and also include the Jacobian.
exercise.solution: The transformed integrand is $(1+u)^{2}v$. Integrating $v$ from 0 to 1 gives $(1+u)^{2}/2$, and integrating $u$ gives $7/6$.
rubric: Transform the field as well as the measure.
Distinguish finite-cell scale from the derivative.

sections.title: Volume is a triple product
sections.text: For $T(u,v,w)$, the signed determinant of its three derivative columns measures oriented volume scale. Scalar volume uses its absolute value. Swapping two parameter columns reverses the sign without changing the physical volume.

sections.title: Order in spherical coordinates
sections.text: With columns ordered $(\rho,\varphi,\theta)$ for $x=\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta$, $y=\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta$, $z=\rho\cos\varphi$, the determinant is $\rho^2\sin\varphi$. The order $(\rho,\theta,\varphi)$ has its negative. Both give the same positive volume factor on the standard interior range.

exercise.prompt: Find the volume scale for $T(u,v,w)=(2u,-3v,4w)$.
exercise.hint: Multiply the diagonal entries.
exercise.solution: The signed determinant is $-24$ and the volume scale is 24. The negative sign records orientation reversal.
rubric: State the coordinate order.
Use absolute value for volume.

sections.title: State the map’s scope
sections.text: A sufficient change-of-variables setting is a one-to-one $C^1$ map on a neighborhood of a region with nonzero determinant, plus an integrable transformed field and ordinary negligible boundaries. The transformed integral uses $f(T(u))|\det DT(u)|$.

sections.title: Local invertibility is not global injectivity
sections.text: The map $(u,v)\mapsto(e^u\cos v,e^u\sin v)$ has nonzero determinant $e^{2u}$, but repeats whenever $v$ increases by $2\pi$. Integrating over two full angle turns counts the image twice. Restrict the parameter range or explicitly account for multiplicity.

exercise.prompt: Why does a polar integral over $\theta\in [0,4\pi]$ double-count a disk?
exercise.hint: Compare points at $\theta$ and $\theta +2\pi$.
exercise.solution: They have identical physical coordinates for each positive $r$, so almost every disk point is covered twice. Using the usual $r$ Jacobian over that interval computes twice the disk integral.
rubric: Check global coverage, not only the determinant.
Explain multiplicity away from negligible seams.

sections.title: Invert at corresponding points
sections.text: For an invertible differentiable map $S=T^{-1}$, $DS(T(u))DT(u)=I$. Thus $\det DS(T(u))=1/\det DT(u)$. The locations matter: reciprocal determinants are evaluated at points related by the map.

sections.title: A nonlinear example
sections.text: For $u=x$ and $v=y/(1+x)$, with $x>-1$, the forward determinant is $1/(1+x)$. The inverse is $x=u,y=(1+u)v$ and its determinant is $1+u$. When integrating in $u$,$v$, use the latter absolute factor.

exercise.prompt: For $u=2x$ and $v=3y$, what factor converts $du dv$ to $dx dy$?
exercise.hint: Compute the inverse map, or reciprocate the nonzero determinant.
exercise.solution: The inverse is $x=u/2,y=v/3$, so dx $dy=(1/6)du$ dv.
rubric: Identify the direction of substitution.
Do not insert the forward determinant 6.

sections.title: Density accumulates with length
sections.text: For a parametrized curve $r(t)$, $\int_C f\,ds=\int f(r(t))|r'(t)|\,dt$. Reversing orientation preserves the value because speed is nonnegative. Repeated traversal repeats the accumulation.

sections.title: Non-unit speed is visible
sections.text: For $r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t)$, speed is $2$. With density $f=3$, one traversal has integral $\int_0^{2\pi}6\,dt=12\pi$. Using $dt$ alone would underestimate by a factor of two.

exercise.prompt: Integrate density $f(x,y)=x$ along $r(t)=(t,2t)$, $0\le t\le 1$.
exercise.hint: The speed is constant $\sqrt{5}$.
exercise.solution: The integral is $\sqrt{5}\int_0^1t\,dt =\sqrt{5}/2$. Reversing the traversal leaves the scalar line integral unchanged.
rubric: Evaluate density along the curve.
Include the speed factor.

sections.title: Components depend on position
sections.text: A vector field $F$ assigns a vector to each point of its domain. For $F=(-y,x)$, arrows are tangential to circles about zero; for $F=(x,y)$, arrows are radial. Arrow normalization improves legibility but hides magnitude unless a scale or readout supplies it.

sections.title: Domain is part of the field
sections.text: The field $(-y/(x^{2}+y^{2}),x/(x^{2}+y^{2}))$ excludes the origin. A plot that omits one arrow does not repair the missing domain point; theorem hypotheses must respect that puncture.

exercise.prompt: At $(1,0)$, compare radial $F=(x,y)$ and rotational $G=(-y,x)$.
exercise.hint: Substitute the point into each component.
exercise.solution: $F=(1,0)$ points outward and $G=(0,1)$ is tangent counterclockwise. Their dot product is zero.
rubric: Evaluate the field at the point.
Distinguish field vector from position vector when they differ.

sections.title: Work uses a signed component
sections.text: Work is $\int F(r(t))\cdot r'(t)dt$. Parallel force and velocity contribute positively, opposed ones negatively, and perpendicular components contribute zero. Unlike a scalar length integral, reversing traversal reverses the sign.

sections.title: A transverse component contributes nothing
sections.text: On $r(t)=(t,0)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, $F=(1,5)$ has dot product 1 with $r'=(1,0)$. Work is 1 despite the large vertical force component. For $F=(-1,5)$, work is $-1$.

exercise.prompt: Find the work of $F=(2,3)$ along the segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,2)$.
exercise.hint: Use $r(t)=(t,2t)$.
exercise.solution: The dot product $(2,3)\cdot (1,2)=8$ is constant, so work is 8. The reverse path gives $-8$.
rubric: Use velocity rather than unit tangent alone.
Retain orientation and sign.

sections.title: Three differentials are one dot product
sections.text: The expression $P$ $dx+Q dy+R$ dz becomes $[P(r)x'+Q(r)y'+R(r)z']dt$. Each differential follows the same parameter interval; none is an independent integration variable.

sections.title: Check terms individually
sections.text: Along $r(t)=(t,t^{2})$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, $\int y dx+x$ dy becomes $\int (t^{2}+2t^{2})dt=1$. The form is $d(xy)$, so endpoints independently give $1-0=1$.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate $\oint(x\,dy-y\,dx)$ around the unit circle counterclockwise.
exercise.hint: Use $x=\cos t$, $y=\sin t$ and differentiate both.
exercise.solution: The integrand becomes $\cos^{2}t+\sin^{2}t=1$, giving $2\pi$ over $[0,2\pi ]$. Reversing orientation gives $-2\pi$.
rubric: Differentiate both coordinates.
Carry the minus sign in dx.

sections.title: Each piece gets its own parameter
sections.text: For a path from A to $B$ to $C$, parametrize both oriented segments and add their integrals. Shared endpoints contribute no interval length. Reversing a piece changes its vector line integral sign but not a scalar length integral.

sections.title: Compare different paths
sections.text: For $F=(y,0)$, from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$, traveling horizontally then vertically gives work 0. Traveling vertically then horizontally gives work 1. The same endpoints do not imply the same work without conservativeness.

exercise.prompt: Compute $\int y\,dx$ along $(0,0)\to(1,0)\to(1,1)$.
exercise.hint: On the first segment $y=0$; on the second $dx=0$.
exercise.solution: Both pieces contribute zero, so the integral is zero. The alternative path through $(0,1)$ gives 1.
rubric: Respect the order and direction of pieces.
Avoid inferring endpoint-only dependence.

sections.title: Circulation is work on a closed traversal
sections.text: For $F=(-y,x)$ and the unit circle counterclockwise, $F(r)=r'$ and the dot product is 1, giving circulation $2\pi$. For the radial field $(x,y)$, it is zero because field and velocity are perpendicular.

sections.title: A field can change the sign around a path
sections.text: For constant $F=(1,0)$ on a circle, local work density is $-\sin t$. Some arcs contribute positively and others negatively, with total zero. Zero net work does not mean every local contribution vanishes.

exercise.prompt: Find circulation of $F=(-2y,2x)$ around a radius-$R$ circle counterclockwise.
exercise.hint: Both field and velocity scale with $R$.
